blocks.html: Complex analysis is calculus with complex numbers, and two tools from earlier courses do most of the bookkeeping. In the complex plane you met the modulus $|a + bi| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$, the distance from $0$, and the conjugate $a - bi$, the mirror image across the real axis. In complex division you multiplied by the conjugate to clear $i$ from a denominator. This lesson makes both tools exact and quick, because every later topic leans on them.

For $z = x + iy$ (with $x, y$ real), the conjugate is $\overline{z} = x - iy$ and the modulus is $|z| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$. Then $$z\overline{z} = |z|^2, \qquad |zw| = |z|\,|w|, \qquad \left|\frac{z}{w}\right| = \frac{|z|}{|w|}, \qquad |z + w| \le |z| + |w|.$$ Also $\overline{z + w} = \overline{z} + \overline{w}$, $\overline{zw} = \overline{z}\,\overline{w}$, $\operatorname{Re} z = \frac{z + \overline{z}}{2}$ and $\operatorname{Im} z = \frac{z - \overline{z}}{2i}$.

Multiply out: $z\overline{z} = (x + iy)(x - iy) = x^2 - (iy)^2 = x^2 + y^2$, a real number that is never negative. That one fact gives the rest. For products, $|zw|^2 = zw\,\overline{zw} = (z\overline{z})(w\overline{w}) = |z|^2|w|^2$. For the triangle inequality,
      $$|z + w|^2 = (z + w)(\overline{z} + \overline{w}) = |z|^2 + 2\operatorname{Re}(z\overline{w}) + |w|^2 \le |z|^2 + 2|z|\,|w| + |w|^2 = (|z| + |w|)^2,$$
      because the real part of a number is at most its modulus. Geometrically: one side of a triangle is never longer than the other two together.

blocks.title: Modulus, conjugate and square
steps: Flip the sign of the imaginary part: $\overline{z} = 3 + 4i$.
Compare: $z^2$ is not real, while $|z|^2 = 25$ is. (Their sizes agree: $|z^2| = \sqrt{49 + 576} = 25 = |z|^2$.)

blocks.title: A modulus without multiplying
steps: $|zw| = |z|\,|w|$, so find the two moduli separately.
The product has modulus $5\sqrt{5}$. (Multiplying out gives $11 + 2i$, and $\sqrt{121 + 4} = \sqrt{125} = 5\sqrt{5}$: the same.)

blocks.html: Treating $z^2$ and $|z|^2$ as the same. For $z = 1 + i$, $z^2 = 1 + 2i + i^2 = 2i$, but $|z|^2 = z\overline{z} = 1 + 1 = 2$. The square of $z$ doubles its angle; the square of its modulus is a length squared. Quick check: $|z|^2$ is always a real number $\ge 0$. If your answer for $|z|^2$ still contains $i$, you multiplied $z$ by itself instead of by $\overline{z}$.

The triangle inequality also runs backwards: $|z + w| \ge \big||z| - |w|\big|$. So if $|z| = 3$ and $|w| = 5$, then $|z + w|$ can be anything from $2$ to $8$, and both ends happen. These two bounds are the main tool for estimating integrals later in the course.

items: Dividing: multiply the top and bottom by $\overline{w}$, so the bottom becomes the real number $|w|^2$.
Solving for $z$: an equation that mixes $z$ and $\overline{z}$ is two real equations; write $z = x + iy$ and match real and imaginary parts.
Estimating: to bound $\left|\frac{1}{z^2 + 4}\right|$ on the circle $|z| = 3$, use $|z^2 + 4| \ge |z|^2 - 4 = 5$, so the fraction is at most $\frac{1}{5}$.

blocks.html: In Precalculus you wrote $z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)$ and found that multiplying complex numbers multiplies their moduli and adds their angles. Calculus gives that rule a short name. The Maclaurin series from known series work for complex inputs too, and they explain why $\cos\theta + i\sin\theta$ deserves to be written as a power of $e$.

Euler's formula: $e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta$. Every nonzero complex number has an exponential form $z = re^{i\theta}$ with $r = |z|$ and $\theta$ an argument (angle) of $z$. Then $$re^{i\alpha} \cdot se^{i\beta} = rs\,e^{i(\alpha + \beta)}, \qquad \frac{re^{i\alpha}}{se^{i\beta}} = \frac{r}{s}e^{i(\alpha - \beta)}, \qquad \left(re^{i\theta}\right)^n = r^ne^{in\theta}.$$

Put $i\theta$ into $e^{x} = \sum \frac{x^n}{n!}$. The powers of $i$ cycle $1, i, -1, -i$, so the even terms are real and the odd terms carry an $i$:
      $$e^{i\theta} = \left(1 - \frac{\theta^2}{2!} + \frac{\theta^4}{4!} - \cdots\right) + i\left(\theta - \frac{\theta^3}{3!} + \frac{\theta^5}{5!} - \cdots\right) = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta.$$
      The product rule is the angle-sum formulas in disguise: $(\cos\alpha + i\sin\alpha)(\cos\beta + i\sin\beta) = \cos(\alpha + \beta) + i\sin(\alpha + \beta)$, which is exactly what $e^{i\alpha}e^{i\beta} = e^{i(\alpha + \beta)}$ says.

Exponential form is the natural way to multiply, divide and take powers; the form $a + bi$ is the natural way to add. Most problems switch between the two. Going from $re^{i\theta}$ to $a + bi$ is direct: $a = r\cos\theta$ and $b = r\sin\theta$. Going the other way needs care with the angle, as the first example shows. Two special values are worth knowing by heart: $e^{i\pi} = -1$ and $e^{2\pi i} = 1$. The second says that a full turn brings you back, so the angle of a complex number is only defined up to adding $2\pi k$; the next lesson deals with that.

blocks.html: Taking the angle straight from $\tan^{-1}\frac{b}{a}$. A calculator's $\tan^{-1}$ only returns angles between $-\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $\frac{\pi}{2}$, so for points on the left half of the plane it points the wrong way: for $-1 - i$ it gives $\frac{\pi}{4}$, the angle of $1 + i$. blocks.html: An angle for $z$ is not unique: adding a full turn $2\pi$ points the same way. Exponential form hid this, because $e^{i\theta} = e^{i(\theta + 2\pi)}$. Before the complex logarithm arrives, we need language for the whole family of angles and a rule for choosing one of them.

For $z \ne 0$, $\arg z$ is the set of all arguments $\theta + 2\pi k$ ($k$ any integer). The principal argument $\operatorname{Arg} z$ is the one value in $(-\pi, \pi]$. Products add arguments as sets, $\arg(zw) = \arg z + \arg w$, but the principal values only satisfy $$\operatorname{Arg}(zw) = \operatorname{Arg} z + \operatorname{Arg} w + 2\pi k, \qquad k \in \{-1, 0, 1\},$$ with $k \ne 0$ exactly when the sum leaves $(-\pi, \pi]$.

If $z = |z|e^{i\alpha}$ and $w = |w|e^{i\beta}$, then $zw = |zw|e^{i(\alpha + \beta)}$, so $\alpha + \beta$ is an argument of $zw$. When $\alpha = \operatorname{Arg} z$ and $\beta = \operatorname{Arg} w$, the sum lies in $(-2\pi, 2\pi]$, which is wider than the principal interval. Shifting it by one full turn (if needed) brings it back. The interval $(-\pi, \pi]$ is a convention: it puts the jump on the negative real axis, and it includes $\pi$ so that negative real numbers have $\operatorname{Arg} = \pi$.

Why care? A function like $\operatorname{Arg}$ has to give one answer per input, so it must make a choice, and every choice has a place where it jumps. For $\operatorname{Arg}$ the jump is on the negative real axis: just above it the value is close to $\pi$, just below it close to $-\pi$. Near that ray, $\operatorname{Arg}$ is not continuous. When we define the complex logarithm by $\operatorname{Log} z = \ln|z| + i\operatorname{Arg} z$, it inherits exactly this jump, and the rules for logarithms inherit the extra $2\pi$.

blocks.title: Principal arguments on the axes
steps: $-4$ lies on the negative real axis: $\operatorname{Arg}(-4) = \pi$ (not $-\pi$, which is excluded).
$-\sqrt{3} + i$ is in quadrant II with reference angle $\tan^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{\pi}{6}$, so $\operatorname{Arg} = \pi - \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{5\pi}{6}$.

blocks.title: When the sum leaves the interval
blocks.q: Let $z = -1 + i$ and $w = -\sqrt{3} + i$. Find $\operatorname{Arg} z + \operatorname{Arg} w$ and $\operatorname{Arg}(zw)$.
steps: $\operatorname{Arg} z = \frac{3\pi}{4}$ and $\operatorname{Arg} w = \frac{5\pi}{6}$; their sum is $\frac{9\pi + 10\pi}{12} = \frac{19\pi}{12}$.
Check: $zw = (-1 + i)(-\sqrt{3} + i) = (\sqrt{3} - 1) - (1 + \sqrt{3})i$, which has a positive real part and a negative imaginary part, so its angle is indeed between $-\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $0$.

blocks.html: Assuming $\operatorname{Arg}(zw) = \operatorname{Arg} z + \operatorname{Arg} w$. For $z = w = -1$, the right side is $\pi + \pi = 2\pi$, but $zw = 1$ and $\operatorname{Arg} 1 = 0$. The set identity $\arg(zw) = \arg z + \arg w$ is fine; the principal values can differ by $2\pi$. Check any answer by asking whether it lies in $(-\pi, \pi]$.

blocks.html: Theorems in complex analysis are stated on regions: "analytic on the disk", "continuous on the closed annulus". The modulus turns most of these sets into geometry, because $|z - a|$ is the distance from $z$ to $a$. This lesson is a short dictionary from inequalities to pictures, plus the words open, closed, bounded and connected.

$|z - a| < r$ is the open disk with center $a$ and radius $r$; $|z - a| \le r$ is the closed disk; $|z - a| = r$ is the circle; $r_1 < |z - a| < r_2$ is an annulus; $\operatorname{Re} z > c$ and $\operatorname{Im} z < c$ are half-planes; $|z - a| = |z - b|$ is the perpendicular bisector of the segment from $a$ to $b$. A set is open if each of its points has a small disk around it inside the set, closed if it contains its boundary, bounded if it fits inside some disk, and connected if any two of its points can be joined by a path inside it. An open connected set is called a region (or domain).

With $z = x + iy$ and $a = a_1 + ia_2$, $|z - a| = \sqrt{(x - a_1)^2 + (y - a_2)^2}$: the distance formula. So "$|z - a| < r$" says "$z$ is less than $r$ away from $a$". Strict inequalities between continuous quantities give open sets (wiggling a point a little keeps the inequality true), while $\le$ and $=$ keep the boundary and give closed sets.

blocks.name: complexplane
blocks.cap: The arrow for $z - w$ is the same length as the segment from $w$ to $z$. So $|z - w|$ is the distance between the two points.

blocks.title: Reading a disk
steps: Rewrite the inside as $z - a$: $z + 1 - 2i = z - (-1 + 2i)$.
So the set is all $z$ at distance at most $3$ from $-1 + 2i$: the closed disk with center $-1 + 2i$ and radius $3$.
It is closed (it includes the circle), bounded and connected, but not open.

blocks.title: Equal distances
steps: The points equally far from $1$ and from $-i$ form the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them.
Algebra: square both sides, $(x - 1)^2 + y^2 = x^2 + (y + 1)^2$.

blocks.title: A circle in disguise
steps: Divide by $3$ and complete the square: $(x - 4)^2 + y^2 = 4$.
A circle with center $4$ and radius $2$. Check: $z = 2$ gives $|2| = 2$ and $2|2 - 3| = 2$.

blocks.html: Reading the sign of the center backwards. $|z - 2i| < 3$ is the disk centered at $2i$, not at $-2i$: the expression is the distance from $z$ to $2i$. And $|z + 2i| < 3$ means $|z - (-2i)| < 3$, centered at $-2i$. To check, plug in your claimed center: it should make the inside $0$.

blocks.html: A complex function $w = f(z)$ takes a complex number and returns one. Since $z = x + iy$ carries two real numbers and so does $w = u + iv$, a complex function is really a pair of real functions of two variables, the kind you studied in multivariable calculus. Splitting $f$ into $u$ and $v$ is the first move in almost every computation of this course.

Write $f(z) = u(x, y) + i\,v(x, y)$, where $u = \operatorname{Re} f$ and $v = \operatorname{Im} f$ are real-valued. For example, for $f(z) = z^2$, $$z^2 = (x + iy)^2 = (x^2 - y^2) + i(2xy), \qquad u = x^2 - y^2, \quad v = 2xy.$$

Substitute $z = x + iy$ and expand, using $i^2 = -1$. Every term is either real or a real number times $i$; collect the real terms into $u$ and the coefficients of $i$ into $v$. The imaginary part is a real function: in $x^2 - y^2 + 2xy\,i$, the imaginary part is $2xy$, the number that multiplies $i$. With a quotient, multiply the top and bottom by the conjugate of the bottom first, so the denominator becomes real.

blocks.name: cplx-domaincolor
blocks.cap: One way to see a complex function: color each point $z$ by the direction of $f(z)$ (red for positive real values, then yellow, green, cyan, blue, magenta going counterclockwise), with brighter rings as $|f(z)|$ grows. For $z^2$ the colors go around twice as you circle $0$, because squaring doubles angles. Drag the probe to read $f(z)$.

blocks.title: A polynomial
steps: Collect: real part $u = x^2 - y^2 - 3y$; coefficient of $i$: $v = 2xy + 3x$.

blocks.title: A quotient
steps: Multiply the top and bottom by $\overline{z} = x - iy$: $\dfrac{1}{x + iy} = \dfrac{x - iy}{x^2 + y^2}$.

blocks.title: A function that uses the conjugate
steps: $u = x^2 + y^2 + x$ and $v = -y$. Formulas like this one are perfectly good functions of $x$ and $y$, but in the next unit we will see that they are not complex differentiable.

blocks.html: Keeping the $i$ inside $v$. From $z^2 = x^2 - y^2 + 2ixy$, some people write $v = 2ixy$. But $v$ is the imaginary part, a real number: $v = 2xy$. A check that always works: $u$ and $v$ should both be real whenever $x$ and $y$ are; no $i$ may appear in either of them.

Evaluating $f$ at a point needs no splitting at all: $f(1 + 2i)$ for $f(z) = z^2 + 3iz$ is $(1 + 2i)^2 + 3i(1 + 2i) = (-3 + 4i) + (-6 + 3i) = -9 + 7i$. As a check, the formulas from the first example give $u(1, 2) = 1 - 4 - 6 = -9$ and $v(1, 2) = 4 + 3 = 7$.

blocks.html: A real function can be drawn as a graph, but the graph of a complex function would need four dimensions. Instead we draw two planes side by side, the $z$-plane and the $w$-plane, and watch where $f$ sends points, curves and regions. The exponential form $z = re^{i\theta}$ makes the basic maps easy to read, because it shows what happens to lengths and to angles separately.

Three maps to know by sight:
• $w = az + b$: multiply by $a$ (turn by $\operatorname{Arg} a$, stretch by $|a|$), then shift by $b$. Lines go to lines and circles to circles.
• $w = z^2$: $re^{i\theta} \mapsto r^2e^{2i\theta}$. Lengths are squared and angles are doubled, so a sector of opening $\alpha$ at $0$ becomes a sector of opening $2\alpha$.
• $w = \frac{1}{z}$: $re^{i\theta} \mapsto \frac{1}{r}e^{-i\theta}$. Points near $0$ go far away and vice versa: the circle $|z| = r$ goes to $|w| = \frac{1}{r}$.

Each statement is the exponential form at work. $(re^{i\theta})^2 = r^2e^{2i\theta}$ squares the modulus and doubles the argument. For $\frac{1}{z}$: $\frac{1}{re^{i\theta}} = \frac{1}{r}e^{-i\theta}$, so the modulus is inverted and the angle changes sign. For $az + b$: with $a = |a|e^{i\varphi}$, $az = |a|r\,e^{i(\theta + \varphi)}$, a rotation by $\varphi$ and a stretch by $|a|$, and adding $b$ slides everything.

blocks.name: cplx-mapping
blocks.cap: The first quadrant (left) and its image under $z^2$ (right): the rays at angles $0$ to $\frac{\pi}{2}$ become rays at $0$ to $\pi$, so the quarter disk becomes a half disk. Drag $z_0$ and watch $w_0 = z_0^2$.

blocks.title: A disk under a linear map
blocks.q: Find the image of the disk $|z - 1| < 2$ under $w = 2iz + 3$.
steps: A linear map sends the center to the center: $2i(1) + 3 = 3 + 2i$.
It stretches every distance by $|2i| = 2$: the radius becomes $4$.
The image is the disk $|w - (3 + 2i)| < 4$, turned a quarter turn (which a disk does not show).

blocks.title: A sector under squaring
blocks.q: Find the image of the sector $0 < \arg z < \frac{\pi}{3}$ under $w = z^2$, and the image of the point $z = 1 + i$.
steps: Squaring doubles angles: the sector becomes $0 < \arg w < \frac{2\pi}{3}$ (lengths $r > 0$ still give every $r^2 > 0$).

blocks.title: A circle under inversion
blocks.q: Under $w = \frac{1}{z}$, where does the circle $|z| = 3$ go, and where does $z = 3i$ go?
steps: $\frac{1}{3i} = \frac{-i}{3}$: the top of the big circle goes to the bottom of the small one (the angle changes sign).

blocks.name: cplx-mapping
blocks.cap: Not every circle stays a circle under $\frac{1}{z}$: this one passes through $0$, and its image is the vertical line $\operatorname{Re} w = \frac{1}{2}$. Unit 8 explains why.

blocks.html: Expecting $z^2$ to send the first quadrant to itself. Squaring keeps real numbers real, so it is tempting to think regions keep their shape. But every angle doubles: the ray at $\frac{\pi}{4}$ goes to the ray at $\frac{\pi}{2}$, and the edge at $\frac{\pi}{2}$ goes to the negative real axis. The first quadrant fills the whole upper half-plane. Check with one point: $(1 + i)^2 = 2i$, already outside the first quadrant.

blocks.html: Limits of complex functions work like limits in two variables: $z$ can approach $z_0$ from any direction and along any curve, not just from the left and the right. That freedom is what makes the complex derivative so demanding, so it is worth seeing clearly first.

$\displaystyle\lim_{z \to z_0} f(z) = L$ means $|f(z) - L|$ can be made as small as we like by taking $0 < |z - z_0|$ small enough, whatever the direction. So if two paths to $z_0$ give two different values, the limit does not exist. $f$ is continuous at $z_0$ when $\lim_{z \to z_0} f(z) = f(z_0)$. Sums, products, quotients (with a nonzero bottom) and compositions of continuous functions are continuous, so polynomials are continuous everywhere.

The definition only mentions the distance $|z - z_0|$, which is the same in every direction, so it cannot prefer one path. In terms of real and imaginary parts, $f(z) \to L$ exactly when $u \to \operatorname{Re} L$ and $v \to \operatorname{Im} L$, because $|f - L|^2 = (u - \operatorname{Re} L)^2 + (v - \operatorname{Im} L)^2$. To show a limit exists, bound $|f(z) - L|$ by something that tends to $0$; to show it does not, find two paths that disagree.

blocks.name: cplx-domaincolor
blocks.cap: $f(z) = \frac{\overline{z}}{z}$ has modulus $1$ everywhere, and its color depends only on the direction from $0$: red along the real axis ($f = 1$), cyan along the imaginary axis ($f = -1$). Every color crowds into $0$, so $f$ has no limit there.

blocks.title: Zero over zero
steps: Substituting gives $\frac{0}{0}$, so $z - 2i$ is a factor of the top: $z^2 + 4 = (z - 2i)(z + 2i)$.
For $z \ne 2i$ the quotient is $z + 2i$, which tends to $4i$.

blocks.title: A limit that does not exist
steps: Two paths, two values: the limit does not exist. (Along the line $y = x$ the value is $\frac{1 - i}{1 + i} = -i$, a third value.)

blocks.title: A limit that does exist
steps: $|z| \to 0$ along every path, so the limit is $0$.

blocks.html: Checking only the real axis, or only straight lines. Agreement along the real axis proves nothing; agreement along every line through $z_0$ still is not enough in general (as in calculus 3, a curve such as a parabola can disagree with all lines). To prove a limit exists, bound $|f(z) - L|$ by a quantity that tends to $0$, such as $|z - z_0|$. To disprove it, two paths with different values are enough.

blocks.html: In Calculus 1 the derivative was the limit of a difference quotient. The complex derivative uses the same quotient, but now the step $h$ is a complex number, so it can shrink to $0$ from every direction. That one change makes complex differentiability far stronger than the real kind.

$f$ is complex differentiable at $z_0$ if $$f'(z_0) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(z_0 + h) - f(z_0)}{h}$$ exists, with $h$ complex and the same limit from every direction. The usual rules hold: sums, products, quotients, the chain rule, and $(z^n)' = nz^{n - 1}$. Near such a point, $f(z_0 + h) \approx f(z_0) + f'(z_0)\,h$: tiny pieces of the plane are turned by $\arg f'(z_0)$ and stretched by $|f'(z_0)|$.

For $f(z) = z^2$: $\frac{(z_0 + h)^2 - z_0^2}{h} = \frac{2z_0h + h^2}{h} = 2z_0 + h$, which tends to $2z_0$ no matter how $h \to 0$. For $f(z) = \overline{z}$: $\frac{\overline{z_0 + h} - \overline{z_0}}{h} = \frac{\overline{h}}{h}$. With $h$ real this is $1$; with $h = it$ it is $\frac{-it}{it} = -1$. The limit depends on the direction, so $\overline{z}$ is differentiable nowhere. The algebra for products, quotients and powers is word for word the same as in real calculus, so those rules carry over.

blocks.name: cplx-mapping
blocks.cap: A small square at $z_0$ and its image under $z^2$: turned and scaled, still nearly a square. Drag $z_0$; the readout gives $f'(z_0)$. Try the conjugate below for comparison.

blocks.name: cplx-mapping
blocks.cap: Under $\overline{z}$ the square is flipped (look at the red edge's arrow). No turn-and-scale does that, so $\overline{z}$ has no complex derivative.

blocks.title: Two directions disagree
blocks.q: For $f(z) = |z|^2$ at $z_0 = 1 + 2i$, compute the limit of the difference quotient along real $h$ and along imaginary $h$.
steps: Divide by $h$: $z_0\frac{\overline{h}}{h} + \overline{z_0} + \frac{|h|^2}{h}$. The last term tends to $0$.
Real $h$: $z_0 + \overline{z_0} = 2$. Imaginary $h$: $-z_0 + \overline{z_0} = -4i$. Different, so $|z|^2$ is not differentiable at $1 + 2i$ (only at $0$, where both are $0$).

blocks.html: Why is "turned and stretched" the right picture? Near $z_0$, the change $f(z_0 + h) - f(z_0)$ is about $f'(z_0)\,h$, and multiplying $h$ by the complex number $f'(z_0) = \rho e^{i\varphi}$ turns it by $\varphi$ and stretches it by $\rho$, the same for every direction of $h$. A real map of the plane can do much more: stretch one direction more than another, shear, or flip. Complex differentiability allows only turning and uniform stretching. That restriction is the source of everything special about analytic functions.

Assuming a smooth formula in $x$ and $y$ must be complex differentiable. $\overline{z} = x - iy$ and $|z|^2 = x^2 + y^2$ have partial derivatives of every order, yet neither has a complex derivative (except $|z|^2$ at the single point $0$). Complex differentiability asks the difference quotient to agree from all directions at once. Quick test: compare $h$ real with $h$ imaginary; if they disagree, $f$ is not differentiable there.

blocks.html: Checking every direction of approach sounds hopeless, but two directions are enough when the partial derivatives of $u$ and $v$ are continuous. Comparing the horizontal and the vertical approach in the difference quotient gives two short equations that test differentiability by computation.

Let $f = u + iv$, with $u$ and $v$ having continuous first partial derivatives near $z_0$. Then $f$ is complex differentiable at $z_0$ exactly when the Cauchy–Riemann equations hold there: $$u_x = v_y, \qquad u_y = -v_x.$$ In that case $f'(z_0) = u_x + iv_x = v_y - iu_y$.

Suppose $f'(z_0)$ exists. With $h$ real, the difference quotient is $\frac{f(z_0 + h) - f(z_0)}{h} \to f_x = u_x + iv_x$. With $h = it$, it becomes $\frac{f(z_0 + it) - f(z_0)}{it} \to \frac{1}{i}f_y = -i(u_y + iv_y) = v_y - iu_y$. Both equal $f'(z_0)$, so $u_x + iv_x = v_y - iu_y$; matching real and imaginary parts gives $u_x = v_y$ and $v_x = -u_y$. The converse (equations plus continuous partials imply differentiability) comes from the linear approximation of $u$ and $v$.

blocks.cap: $f = x^2 + iy^2$ satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations only on the line $y = x$. Put $z_0$ on that line and the little square stays a square; move it off and the square is stretched unevenly.

blocks.title: Checking a function
blocks.q: Show that $f = x^2 - y^2 + 2x + i(2xy + 2y)$ satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations everywhere, and find $f'(z)$.

blocks.title: Finding the constants
blocks.q: For which real $p$ and $q$ is $u + iv = (x^3 + pxy^2) + i(qx^2y - y^3)$ differentiable everywhere?
steps: $u_x = 3x^2 + py^2$ and $v_y = qx^2 - 3y^2$. For these to agree for all $x, y$: $q = 3$ and $p = -3$.
Second equation: $u_y = 2pxy$ and $-v_x = -2qxy$, so $p = -q$, which holds.

blocks.title: Differentiable on a line only
blocks.q: Where is $f = x^2 + iy^2$ complex differentiable?
steps: The first equation needs $x = y$. So $f$ is differentiable exactly on the line $y = x$, with $f' = u_x + iv_x = 2x$ there.

items: Write $f = u + iv$ and compute the four partials $u_x$, $u_y$, $v_x$, $v_y$.
Find where both $u_x = v_y$ and $u_y = -v_x$ hold. If the partials are continuous, $f$ is complex differentiable exactly there.
At those points, $f' = u_x + iv_x$. If the equations hold on a whole open set, $f$ is analytic there (next lesson).

blocks.html: Dropping the minus sign, or trusting a single point. The second equation is $u_y = -v_x$; with $u_y = v_x$ instead, $z^2$ would fail the test and $\overline{z}^2$ would pass, which is backwards. Second trap: the equations holding at one point give differentiability at that point only. $|z|^2 = x^2 + y^2$ satisfies them only at $0$ ($u_x = 2x = 0 = v_y$ and $u_y = 2y = 0 = -v_x$), so it is differentiable at $0$ but analytic nowhere, as the next lesson explains.

blocks.html: Differentiability at isolated points, like $|z|^2$ at $0$, is not much use. The useful notion asks for a derivative on a whole open set, and it turns out to be extremely strong: such functions have derivatives of every order and equal their power series. This lesson names them and shows how to find where a formula is analytic, using the Cauchy–Riemann equations and the chain rule.

$f$ is analytic (also called holomorphic) on an open set $U$ if it is complex differentiable at every point of $U$; it is analytic at a point if it is analytic on some disk around it. A function analytic on the whole plane is entire. Polynomials, $e^z$, $\sin z$ and $\cos z$ are entire, and sums, products and compositions of analytic functions are analytic; a quotient $\frac{g}{h}$ is analytic wherever $g$ and $h$ are and $h \ne 0$.

The derivative rules prove the closure statements: if $g$ and $h$ have derivatives at every point of $U$, so do $g + h$, $gh$, and $\frac{g}{h}$ (where $h \ne 0$), with the familiar formulas. For a composition, the chain rule $(g \circ h)' = g'(h(z))\,h'(z)$ works exactly as in real calculus. The word "open" matters: analytic at $z_0$ asks for a whole disk around $z_0$, which is why $|z|^2$, differentiable at the single point $0$, is analytic nowhere.

blocks.cap: $\frac{z + 1}{z^2 + 1}$: the colors flow smoothly everywhere except at $\pm i$, where the bottom is $0$ and all the colors meet. Around the zero at $-1$ they run counterclockwise; around the two poles, clockwise.

blocks.title: Where is it analytic?
steps: The top and the bottom are polynomials, analytic everywhere.
The bottom is $0$ when $z^2 = -1$, that is $z = i$ or $z = -i$.
So $f$ is analytic on the plane with the two points $\pm i$ removed. Note that $z^2 + 1$ has no real zeros, which is exactly why these points are easy to miss.

blocks.title: Zeros of a cubic
steps: $g$ fails to be analytic at $0$, $2$ and $-2$, and is analytic everywhere else.

blocks.title: Zeros of an exponential
steps: Where $e^z = 1$. Writing $z = x + iy$: $|e^z| = e^x = 1$ forces $x = 0$, and $e^{iy} = 1$ forces $y = 2\pi k$.
So at $z = 2\pi ik$ for every integer $k$: infinitely many points on the imaginary axis.

blocks.html: Forgetting the complex zeros of a denominator. $\frac{z + 1}{z^2 + 1}$ looks harmless if you only think of real $z$, but it is not analytic at $\pm i$. When deciding where a quotient is analytic, solve "bottom $= 0$" over the complex numbers, including non-real solutions.

blocks.html: The real and imaginary parts of an analytic function are not arbitrary. Differentiating the Cauchy–Riemann equations once more (using mixed partials) shows that each of them solves Laplace's equation, the equation of steady heat flow and electrostatics. This link is one reason complex analysis matters in physics.

A real function $u(x, y)$ with continuous second partials is harmonic if $u_{xx} + u_{yy} = 0$. If $f = u + iv$ is analytic, then $u$ and $v$ are harmonic. Conversely, if $u$ is harmonic on a disk, there is a harmonic conjugate $v$ (unique up to adding a constant) with $u + iv$ analytic; find it from $v_y = u_x$ and $v_x = -u_y$.

From $u_x = v_y$, differentiate in $x$: $u_{xx} = v_{yx}$. From $u_y = -v_x$, differentiate in $y$: $u_{yy} = -v_{xy}$. Mixed partials are equal (an analytic function has continuous partials of all orders, proved later in the course), so $u_{xx} + u_{yy} = v_{yx} - v_{xy} = 0$. The same argument works for $v$.

blocks.name: surface
blocks.cap: $u = x^2 - y^2 = \operatorname{Re}(z^2)$ is a saddle: curving up in one direction exactly as much as it curves down in the other, so $u_{xx} + u_{yy} = 2 - 2 = 0$. A harmonic function has no peaks or pits inside its domain.

blocks.title: Testing for harmonic
blocks.q: Is $u = x^3 - 3xy^2 + y$ harmonic? Is $u = x^2 + y^2$?
steps: First: $u_{xx} = 6x$ and $u_{yy} = -6x$, so the sum is $0$: harmonic (it is $\operatorname{Re}(z^3 - iz)$).
Second: $u_{xx} + u_{yy} = 2 + 2 = 4 \ne 0$: not harmonic, so $x^2 + y^2$ is not the real part of any analytic function.

blocks.title: Finding a harmonic conjugate
blocks.q: Find $v$ with $v(0, 0) = 0$ so that $u + iv$ is analytic, for $u = x^2 - y^2 + 3x$.
steps: $v_y = u_x = 2x + 3$. Integrate in $y$: $v = 2xy + 3y + g(x)$, where $g$ is any function of $x$ (it disappears when we differentiate in $y$).
$v_x = 2y + g'(x)$ must equal $-u_y = 2y$, so $g'(x) = 0$ and $g$ is a constant.
$v(0, 0) = 0$ makes the constant $0$: $v = 2xy + 3y$. Check: $u + iv = z^2 + 3z$.

blocks.title: An exponential example
blocks.q: Find the harmonic conjugate of $u = e^x\cos y$ with $v(0, 0) = 0$.
steps: $v_y = u_x = e^x\cos y$, so $v = e^x\sin y + g(x)$.
$v_x = e^x\sin y + g'(x)$ must equal $-u_y = e^x\sin y$, so $g$ is constant, and $v(0, 0) = 0$ makes it $0$.
$v = e^x\sin y$, and $u + iv = e^x(\cos y + i\sin y) = e^z$.

blocks.html: Euler's formula defined $e^{i\theta}$ for real $\theta$. Combining it with the ordinary $e^x$ gives the exponential of any complex number. The result is entire, is its own derivative, and has one feature the real exponential lacks: it repeats.

For $z = x + iy$, $\;e^z = e^x(\cos y + i\sin y)$. Then $|e^z| = e^x$, $y$ is an argument of $e^z$, $e^z \ne 0$ for every $z$, $e^{z + w} = e^ze^w$, $(e^z)' = e^z$, and
      $$e^{z + 2\pi i} = e^z,$$
      so $e^z$ is periodic with period $2\pi i$. The equation $e^z = w$ (with $w \ne 0$) has infinitely many solutions $z = \ln|w| + i(\theta + 2\pi k)$, where $\theta$ is any argument of $w$.

The definition is the only one that keeps $e^{x + iy} = e^xe^{iy}$. With $u = e^x\cos y$ and $v = e^x\sin y$: $u_x = e^x\cos y = v_y$ and $u_y = -e^x\sin y = -v_x$, so the Cauchy–Riemann equations hold everywhere and $(e^z)' = u_x + iv_x = e^z$. Since $\cos$ and $\sin$ have period $2\pi$ in $y$, so does $e^z$ in the imaginary direction. To solve $e^z = w$, match moduli ($e^x = |w|$, so $x = \ln|w|$) and angles ($y$ equals an argument of $w$, which is only fixed up to $2\pi k$).

blocks.name: cplx-mapping
blocks.cap: $e^z$ sends the horizontal strip $0 < \operatorname{Im} z < \pi$ onto the upper half-plane: each horizontal line goes to a ray from $0$, each vertical segment to a half circle. Shifting the strip up by $2\pi$ would land on the same picture again.

blocks.title: Solving an equation
steps: $z = \ln 2 + (2k + 1)\pi i$ for every integer $k$: for example $\ln 2 + \pi i$ and $\ln 2 - \pi i$.

blocks.title: Modulus and argument
steps: An argument is $y = -4$ (radians; it is not in $(-\pi, \pi]$, but $-4 + 2\pi$ is, if the principal value is needed).

blocks.html: The picture is worth remembering. A vertical line $\operatorname{Re} z = c$ goes to the circle $|w| = e^c$, traced once for every vertical step of $2\pi$; a horizontal line $\operatorname{Im} z = d$ goes to the ray from $0$ at angle $d$. So every nonzero $w$ is hit, and hit infinitely often, once in each horizontal strip of height $2\pi$. Only $w = 0$ is missed.

Expecting $e^z = w$ to have one solution. In real calculus $e^x = 5$ has exactly one solution. In the complex plane $e^z$ repeats every $2\pi i$, so if $z_0$ is a solution, so are $z_0 \pm 2\pi i$, $z_0 \pm 4\pi i$, and so on. Check your list: all solutions share one real part and differ by multiples of $2\pi i$. (And $e^z = 0$ has no solution at all, since $|e^z| = e^x > 0$.)

blocks.html: Euler's formula gives $\cos\theta = \frac{e^{i\theta} + e^{-i\theta}}{2}$ for real $\theta$. Using the complex exponential, the same formulas define sine and cosine for every complex $z$. On the imaginary axis they turn into the hyperbolic functions, and that is where the surprises live.

$$\cos z = \frac{e^{iz} + e^{-iz}}{2}, \qquad \sin z = \frac{e^{iz} - e^{-iz}}{2i}.$$ Both are entire, with $(\sin z)' = \cos z$ and $(\cos z)' = -\sin z$; the usual identities ($\sin^2 z + \cos^2 z = 1$, the sum formulas) still hold. On the imaginary axis, $\cos(iy) = \cosh y$ and $\sin(iy) = i\sinh y$, and in general $$\sin(x + iy) = \sin x\cosh y + i\cos x\sinh y, \qquad |\sin z|^2 = \sin^2 x + \sinh^2 y.$$ So $\sin z$ and $\cos z$ are unbounded: they take every complex value, including $2$.

Put $z = iy$: $\cos(iy) = \frac{e^{-y} + e^{y}}{2} = \cosh y$ and $\sin(iy) = \frac{e^{-y} - e^{y}}{2i} = i\,\frac{e^y - e^{-y}}{2} = i\sinh y$. The sum formula $\sin(x + iy) = \sin x\cos(iy) + \cos x\sin(iy)$ then gives the rectangular form. For the modulus, $|\sin z|^2 = \sin^2 x\cosh^2 y + \cos^2 x\sinh^2 y$; replace $\cosh^2 y$ by $1 + \sinh^2 y$ and use $\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1$.

blocks.cap: $\sin z$ on a window. On the real axis (blue graph) its size never passes $1$; up the imaginary axis (orange) $|\sin(iy)| = |\sinh y|$ grows like $\frac{1}{2}e^{|y|}$. The zeros sit only at $0, \pm\pi, \ldots$ on the real axis.

steps: $e^{iz} = 2$ gives $iz = \ln 2 + 2\pi ik$, so $z = 2\pi k - i\ln 2$; $e^{iz} = \frac{1}{2}$ gives $z = 2\pi k + i\ln 2$.
All solutions: $z = 2\pi k \pm i\ln 2$. No real solution exists, as expected.

No longer true
blocks.cap: Which facts from the real line carry over. The identities survive because they are polynomial identities in $e^{iz}$; the inequalities came from the unit circle and do not.

blocks.html: The hyperbolic functions extend the same way, $\cosh z = \frac{e^z + e^{-z}}{2}$ and $\sinh z = \frac{e^z - e^{-z}}{2}$, and the two families are the same functions turned a quarter turn: $\cos(iz) = \cosh z$ and $\sin(iz) = i\sinh z$ for every complex $z$. So $\cosh$ is periodic with period $2\pi i$, and $\cosh z = 0$ at $z = \frac{\pi i}{2} + k\pi i$.
Because $|\sin z|$ grows like $\frac{1}{2}e^{|\operatorname{Im} z|}$, any estimate that uses $|\sin z| \le 1$ off the real axis is wrong, a common source of errors when bounding contour integrals.

Carrying $|\sin z| \le 1$ over from the real line. The bound comes from the unit circle, which only describes real angles. Off the real axis, $|\sin(x + iy)|^2 = \sin^2 x + \sinh^2 y$, and $\sinh y$ is unbounded: $|\sin(10i)| = \sinh 10 \approx 11{,}013$. Check any claim of boundedness on the imaginary axis first. (Liouville's theorem, later, says a bounded entire function must be constant, so $\sin z$ could not have been bounded.)

blocks.html: The logarithm should undo the exponential: $\log w$ is a number $z$ with $e^z = w$. But the complex exponential repeats every $2\pi i$, so $e^z = w$ has infinitely many solutions. The logarithm therefore has infinitely many values, one for each choice of argument.

For $z \ne 0$, $$\log z = \ln|z| + i\arg z = \ln|z| + i(\operatorname{Arg} z + 2\pi k), \quad k = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \ldots$$ is the set of all logarithms; its values are $2\pi i$ apart. The principal logarithm is the single value $\operatorname{Log} z = \ln|z| + i\operatorname{Arg} z$, with imaginary part in $(-\pi, \pi]$. Always $e^{\log z} = z$, but $\operatorname{Log}(e^z) = z$ only when $-\pi < \operatorname{Im} z \le \pi$, and $\operatorname{Log}(zw)$ can differ from $\operatorname{Log} z + \operatorname{Log} w$ by $\pm 2\pi i$.

Write $z = |z|e^{i\theta}$ and look for $w = a + ib$ with $e^w = z$. Then $e^a e^{ib} = |z|e^{i\theta}$: the moduli give $e^a = |z|$, so $a = \ln|z|$, and the angles give $b = \theta + 2\pi k$. Every choice of $k$ works, which is why $\log z$ is a set. Choosing the principal argument picks one value; that choice is what makes $\operatorname{Log}$ a function, and its price is the $2\pi$ correction inherited from $\operatorname{Arg}$.

blocks.cap: Left: drag $z$ or send it around $0$. Right: the values $\ln|z| + i(\operatorname{Arg} z + 2\pi k)$, a ladder of points $2\pi$ apart; the principal value ($k = 0$) is circled. Each lap around $0$ moves the gold point one rung.

blocks.title: All the values
blocks.q: List the values of $\log(-3)$ with imaginary part between $-4\pi$ and $4\pi$.
steps: $\ln|-3| = \ln 3$, and the arguments of $-3$ are $\pi + 2\pi k$.

blocks.title: A product rule that fails
steps: They differ by $2\pi i$. As sets, $\log(zw) = \log z + \log w$ is true; for principal values it can fail.

blocks.html: For a positive real number $x$, $\operatorname{Log} x = \ln x$, so the principal logarithm extends the familiar one. The new values are the extra imaginary parts: $\log x = \ln x + 2\pi ki$. Off the cut, $\operatorname{Log}$ is analytic with derivative $\frac{1}{z}$ (next lesson), which is what makes it useful in calculus.
Logarithms with other bases follow: $\log_b z = \frac{\log z}{\log b}$ for a chosen value of $\log b$. They are rarely needed in complex analysis, where "log" always means the natural logarithm.

Giving $\log z$ one value, or using $\operatorname{Log}(zw) = \operatorname{Log} z + \operatorname{Log} w$ blindly. Unless a problem says "principal", $\log z$ means the whole set $\ln|z| + i(\theta + 2\pi k)$. And the product rule for $\operatorname{Log}$ is off by $2\pi i$ whenever $\operatorname{Arg} z + \operatorname{Arg} w$ leaves $(-\pi, \pi]$, as with $\operatorname{Log}(-1) + \operatorname{Log}(-1) = 2\pi i \ne 0 = \operatorname{Log} 1$. Check: exponentiate your answer; every correct value of $\log z$ gives back $z$.

blocks.html: To do calculus with the logarithm we need a function, not a set of values, and we need it to be continuous. A branch picks one value of $\log z$ at each point in a way that varies continuously. Every branch must leave out a curve from $0$ to $\infty$ (a branch cut), because going once around $0$ changes any continuous choice of argument by $2\pi$. The cut is a region boundary that we choose.

$\operatorname{Log} z$ is continuous, and analytic with $(\operatorname{Log} z)' = \frac{1}{z}$, on the plane with the ray $(-\infty, 0]$ removed. Across that cut it jumps by $2\pi i$: at $-a$ ($a > 0$) the values from above tend to $\ln a + \pi i$ and from below to $\ln a - \pi i$.
      Choosing arguments in $(\alpha, \alpha + 2\pi]$ instead gives another branch, with its cut along the ray at angle $\alpha$. Likewise, $\operatorname{Log}(g(z))$ is analytic except where $g(z)$ is a real number $\le 0$.

$\operatorname{Arg} z$ is continuous everywhere except on the negative real axis, where it jumps from near $\pi$ to near $-\pi$; $\ln|z|$ is continuous for $z \ne 0$. So $\operatorname{Log}$ is continuous off the cut. There it is the inverse of $e^w$ on the strip $-\pi < \operatorname{Im} w < \pi$, and the inverse function rule gives $\frac{d}{dz}\operatorname{Log} z = \frac{1}{e^w} = \frac{1}{z}$. No continuous branch can live on a whole circle around $0$: following it once around would change the argument by $2\pi$, so the value could not match up when you return.

blocks.title: Approaching the cut
blocks.q: Find the limits of $\operatorname{Log} z$ as $z \to -4$ from above and from below.
steps: From above, $\operatorname{Arg} z \to \pi$; from below, $\operatorname{Arg} z \to -\pi$.
The limits are $\ln 4 + \pi i$ and $\ln 4 - \pi i$: a jump of $2\pi i$.

blocks.title: Another branch
blocks.q: The branch $F$ of $\log z$ with arguments in $(0, 2\pi]$ has its cut on the positive real axis. Find $F(-1)$ and $F(-i)$.
steps: $\operatorname{Arg}(-i) = -\frac{\pi}{2}$, which is not in $(0, 2\pi]$; adding $2\pi$ gives $\frac{3\pi}{2}$.

blocks.title: Where is a composition analytic?
steps: $\operatorname{Log} w$ fails exactly when $w$ is real and $w \le 0$.
$2z + 6$ is real and $\le 0$ exactly when $z$ is real and $z \le -3$.
So the function is analytic on the plane minus the ray $(-\infty, -3]$, with derivative $\frac{2}{2z + 6} = \frac{1}{z + 3}$.

blocks.html: Two opposite errors. (1) Treating $\operatorname{Log} z$ as analytic everywhere except $0$: it is not even continuous on the negative real axis, so, for example, it cannot serve as an antiderivative of $\frac{1}{z}$ along a loop around $0$. (2) Thinking the cut belongs to the logarithm itself: the many-valued $\log z$ has no cut; a cut is a choice we make to get a single-valued branch, and a different choice gives a different branch. Check by asking: on which set is the formula I wrote continuous?

blocks.html: In real algebra, $a^c = e^{c\ln a}$ for $a > 0$. The same recipe defines powers of complex numbers, with the complex logarithm in place of $\ln$. Because $\log z$ has many values, so does $z^c$, and the familiar exponent rules need care.

For $z \ne 0$ and any complex $c$, $\;z^c = e^{c\log z}$, one value for each value of $\log z$. The principal value is $e^{c\operatorname{Log} z} = |z|^ce^{ic\operatorname{Arg} z}$ (for real $c$).
• $c$ an integer: one value (the usual power).
• $c = \frac{p}{q}$ in lowest terms: exactly $q$ values (the $q$th roots of $z^p$).
• $c$ irrational or not real: infinitely many values. For example, $i^i = e^{i \cdot i(\frac{\pi}{2} + 2\pi k)} = e^{-\frac{\pi}{2} - 2\pi k}$, all of them real.

The values of $\log z$ differ by $2\pi ik$, so the values of $z^c$ differ by factors $e^{2\pi ick}$. If $c$ is an integer, these factors are all $1$. If $c = \frac{p}{q}$, they are the $q$th roots of unity $e^{2\pi ipk/q}$, which repeat after $q$ steps. Otherwise $e^{2\pi ick}$ never repeats, giving infinitely many values. For $i^i$: $\log i = i\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + 2\pi k\right)$, and multiplying by $i$ gives the real number $-\frac{\pi}{2} - 2\pi k$.

steps: The real cube root $-2$ is one of the three values (with $k = 1$), but it is not the principal one.

items: Find $|z|$ and $\operatorname{Arg} z$ (or, for all values, $\operatorname{Arg} z + 2\pi k$).
Form $c\log z = c\ln|z| + ic(\operatorname{Arg} z + 2\pi k)$.
Exponentiate: $z^c = e^{c\log z}$. For real $c$ this is $|z|^ce^{ic(\operatorname{Arg} z + 2\pi k)}$.
Count the distinct values: one for integer $c$, $q$ for $c = \frac{p}{q}$ in lowest terms, infinitely many otherwise.

blocks.html: The principal power $z^c$ is analytic wherever $\operatorname{Log} z$ is (off the negative real axis), with derivative $cz^{c - 1}$ using the same branch.

Using real exponent rules on principal values. Rules like $(zw)^c = z^cw^c$ and $(z^a)^b = z^{ab}$ can fail. With principal values, $\big((-1)(-1)\big)^{1/2} = 1^{1/2} = 1$, but $(-1)^{1/2}(-1)^{1/2} = i \cdot i = -1$. And $\big((-1)^2\big)^{1/2} = 1$ while $(-1)^{2 \cdot \frac{1}{2}} = -1$. Work from the definition $z^c = e^{c\operatorname{Log} z}$ each time, and check your answer by raising it back to the needed power.

blocks.html: Complex integrals are taken along curves in the plane, just like the line integrals of vector calculus. Before integrating anything we need the curves themselves, written as $z(t) = x(t) + iy(t)$. Two shapes do almost all the work in this course: segments and circles, and exponential form makes circles especially short to write.

A contour is a piecewise smooth curve $z(t)$, $a \le t \le b$, with a direction (from $z(a)$ to $z(b)$).
• Segment from $z_1$ to $z_2$: $z(t) = z_1 + t(z_2 - z_1)$, $0 \le t \le 1$, with $z'(t) = z_2 - z_1$.
• Circle $|z - a| = r$, once counterclockwise: $z(t) = a + re^{it}$, $0 \le t \le 2\pi$, with $z'(t) = ire^{it}$.
• The same circle clockwise: $z(t) = a + re^{-it}$.
The length is $\int_a^b |z'(t)|\,dt$; for the circle it is $2\pi r$. The symbol $\oint_C$ means a closed contour traced once counterclockwise unless stated otherwise.

$e^{it} = \cos t + i\sin t$ is the point at angle $t$ on the unit circle, so $re^{it}$ is on the circle of radius $r$ and $a + re^{it}$ on the circle centered at $a$. As $t$ grows, the angle grows: counterclockwise. Replacing $t$ by $-t$ reverses the direction. The derivative $z'(t) = ire^{it}$ is the radius vector $re^{it}$ turned a quarter turn by the factor $i$: tangent to the circle, as a velocity should be, with speed $|z'(t)| = r$.

blocks.name: cplx-contour
blocks.cap: A circle contour with arrows showing its direction. Drag the center or the edge handle. (The readout integrates $f(z) = z$, which you will learn to predict in the next lessons.)

blocks.title: A segment
blocks.q: Parametrize the segment from $1 + i$ to $3 - 2i$.
steps: Check: $z(0) = 1 + i$ and $z(1) = 3 - 2i$. Its length is $|2 - 3i| = \sqrt{13}$.

blocks.title: A point on a circle
steps: $e^{i\pi/2} = i$, so $z\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = 2i + 3i = 5i$: the top of the circle centered at $2i$ with radius $3$.
$z'(t) = 3ie^{it}$, so $z'\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = 3i \cdot i = -3$: at the top, the motion is to the left, which is counterclockwise.

blocks.title: A closed path in two pieces
blocks.q: Describe the boundary of the upper half-disk of radius $2$, traced counterclockwise, and find its length.
steps: Piece 1: the segment from $-2$ to $2$, $z(t) = t$ for $-2 \le t \le 2$.
Piece 2: the upper half circle from $2$ back to $-2$, $z(t) = 2e^{it}$ for $0 \le t \le \pi$.
Length: $4 + 2\pi$. This shape is used later to evaluate integrals over the whole real line.

blocks.html: Using the counterclockwise formula for a clockwise path. $a + re^{it}$ always runs counterclockwise. If a problem asks for clockwise (or "negatively oriented"), use $a + re^{-it}$, or keep $e^{it}$ and run $t$ from $2\pi$ down to $0$. Reversing the direction flips the sign of every contour integral, so this is not a cosmetic choice. Check by computing $z'(0)$: for counterclockwise motion it points straight up from the rightmost point.

blocks.html: The integral of $f$ along a contour is built like a work integral: chop the curve into small pieces, multiply the value of $f$ by the small step $dz$, and add. Parametrizing turns it into an ordinary integral in $t$.

$$\int_C f(z)\,dz = \int_a^b f\big(z(t)\big)\,z'(t)\,dt.$$
      The answer does not depend on how $C$ is parametrized, only on the curve and its direction; reversing the direction changes the sign. The most important single integral: for any circle $C$ centered at $a$, traced once counterclockwise,
      $$\oint_C \frac{dz}{z - a} = 2\pi i, \qquad \oint_C (z - a)^n\,dz = 0 \quad (n \ne -1).$$

$dz = z'(t)\,dt$ is the small step along the curve, just as $d\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}'(t)\,dt$ in a line integral; a change of parameter rescales $dt$ and $z'(t)$ in opposite ways, which is why the parametrization does not matter. For the key integral, put $z = a + re^{it}$: then $(z - a)^n z'(t) = r^ne^{int} \cdot ire^{it} = ir^{n + 1}e^{i(n + 1)t}$. If $n = -1$ this is the constant $i$, and integrating over $[0, 2\pi]$ gives $2\pi i$. Otherwise $\int_0^{2\pi} e^{i(n + 1)t}\,dt = 0$, since cosine and sine integrate to $0$ over whole periods.

blocks.name: cplx-contour
blocks.cap: $\oint \frac{dz}{z}$ around circles: the numerical value stays $2\pi i \approx 6.283i$ however you resize the circle, as long as it goes around $0$. Tick the box to see the wrong value you get by leaving out $z'(t)$.

blocks.title: A segment
blocks.q: Compute $\displaystyle\int_C z^2\,dz$ along the segment from $0$ to $1 + i$.
steps: $(1 + i)^3 = (1 + i)(2i) = -2 + 2i$, so the integral is $-\frac{2}{3} + \frac{2}{3}i$.

blocks.title: Half of a circle
blocks.q: Compute $\displaystyle\int_C \frac{dz}{z}$ along the upper half of $|z| = 1$ from $1$ to $-1$.
steps: $\int_0^\pi i\,dt = \pi i$. The lower half from $1$ to $-1$ gives $-\pi i$: the integral depends on the path.

items: Parametrize: $z(t)$ for $a \le t \le b$, in the right direction; compute $z'(t)$.
Substitute: $f(z(t))\,z'(t)$ is an ordinary complex-valued function of $t$.
Integrate the real and imaginary parts (or integrate $e^{ikt}$ directly).
For a path made of pieces, add the integrals of the pieces.

blocks.html: Contour integrals are linear ($\int_C (af + bg)\,dz = a\int_C f\,dz + b\int_C g\,dz$) and add over pieces of a path, exactly like line integrals.

Leaving out $z'(t)$. Writing $\int f(z(t))\,dt$ treats the integral as an average over the parameter, not a sum of $f\,dz$. For $\oint_{|z| = 1}\frac{dz}{z}$ it gives $\int_0^{2\pi} e^{-it}\,dt = 0$ instead of $2\pi i$. Quick check: the integral of the constant $1$ over a segment from $z_1$ to $z_2$ must be $z_2 - z_1$; that only comes out right with the factor $z'(t)$.

blocks.html: Many contour integrals cannot be computed exactly, but we often only need to know they are small. The ML inequality gives a quick upper bound from two numbers: how big $f$ gets on the curve, and how long the curve is. It rests on the triangle inequality and the definition of the contour integral.

If $|f(z)| \le M$ at every point of $C$ and $C$ has length $L$, then $$\left|\int_C f(z)\,dz\right| \le M \cdot L.$$ To find $M$ for a fraction, bound the top from above and the bottom from below; the reverse triangle inequality $|z^2 + a^2| \ge |z|^2 - a^2$ is the usual tool.

The modulus of a sum is at most the sum of the moduli, and integrals are limits of sums, so $\left|\int_a^b g(t)\,dt\right| \le \int_a^b |g(t)|\,dt$ for complex $g$. Then
      $$\left|\int_C f\,dz\right| = \left|\int_a^b f(z(t))z'(t)\,dt\right| \le \int_a^b |f(z(t))|\,|z'(t)|\,dt \le M\int_a^b |z'(t)|\,dt = M \cdot L.$$

blocks.name: cplx-contour
blocks.cap: The upper half-disk of radius $R$ for $\frac{1}{z^2 + 1}$. The readout splits the integral into the straight piece and the arc, and shows the ML bound $\frac{\pi R}{R^2 - 1}$ for the arc. Drag the handle outward: the arc's share and its bound both shrink toward $0$, while the total stays $\pi$.

blocks.title: A full circle
steps: $M \cdot L = \frac{6\pi}{8} = \frac{3\pi}{4}$. (The true value is $0$, as the residue theorem will show; a bound only promises "no bigger than".)

blocks.title: An arc that vanishes
blocks.q: Show that $\displaystyle\int_{C_R} \frac{dz}{z^2 + 4} \to 0$ as $R \to \infty$, where $C_R$ is the upper half of $|z| = R$.
steps: So the arc contributes nothing in the limit. This is the step that lets residues compute integrals over the real line.

blocks.title: A segment
blocks.q: Bound $\left|\displaystyle\int_C z^2\,dz\right|$ along the segment from $0$ to $3 + 4i$.
steps: $M \cdot L = 125$. (The exact value is $\frac{(3 + 4i)^3}{3}$, with modulus $\frac{125}{3}$, comfortably below the bound.)

blocks.html: Useful lengths: a segment from $z_1$ to $z_2$ has $L = |z_2 - z_1|$; a full circle of radius $R$ has $L = 2\pi R$; an arc of angle $\varphi$ has $L = R\varphi$. For $M$, find the largest value of the top and the smallest value of the bottom on the curve, using the triangle inequality in the right direction for each.

Bounding the denominator in the wrong direction. To bound $\frac{1}{|z^2 + 1|}$ from above you need $|z^2 + 1|$ from below. The triangle inequality $|z^2 + 1| \le R^2 + 1$ gives $\frac{1}{|z^2 + 1|} \ge \frac{1}{R^2 + 1}$, a lower bound for the fraction, useless here. Use $|z^2 + 1| \ge R^2 - 1$ instead. Check: your $M$ should be at least as large as $|f|$ at the worst point you can find (here $z = \pm iR$, where $|f| = \frac{1}{R^2 - 1}$).

blocks.html: For gradient fields, the fundamental theorem for line integrals let you skip the parametrization: the integral is the change in a potential. Contour integrals have the same shortcut whenever $f$ has an antiderivative.

If $F$ is analytic on an open set containing $C$ and $F' = f$ there, then $$\int_C f(z)\,dz = F(z_{\text{end}}) - F(z_{\text{start}}).$$ The integral depends only on the endpoints, and around any closed contour in that set it is $0$. Polynomials, $e^z$, $\sin z$ and $\cos z$ have antiderivatives on the whole plane; $(z - a)^n$ for $n \ne -1$ has one away from $a$. But $\frac{1}{z}$ has no antiderivative on any set that contains a loop around $0$, since $\oint \frac{dz}{z} = 2\pi i \ne 0$.

Along the contour, the chain rule gives $\frac{d}{dt}F(z(t)) = F'(z(t))\,z'(t) = f(z(t))\,z'(t)$. Integrate both sides from $a$ to $b$ with the ordinary fundamental theorem of calculus: $\int_a^b f(z(t))z'(t)\,dt = F(z(b)) - F(z(a))$. The candidate antiderivative for $\frac{1}{z}$ is a branch of $\log z$, but every branch has a cut, and a loop around $0$ must cross it.

blocks.name: cplx-contour
blocks.cap: A path from $0$ to $1 + i$ for $f(z) = z^2$. Drag the corner points anywhere: the value stays $\frac{(1 + i)^3}{3} = -\frac{2}{3} + \frac{2}{3}i$, because $\frac{z^3}{3}$ is an antiderivative on the whole plane.

blocks.title: A polynomial
blocks.q: Compute $\displaystyle\int_C (3z^2 + 2z)\,dz$ along any path from $i$ to $2$.

blocks.title: An exponential
blocks.q: Compute $\displaystyle\int_C e^{\pi z}\,dz$ along any path from $0$ to $i$.

blocks.title: Path dependence for a non-analytic integrand
blocks.q: Compute $\displaystyle\int_C \operatorname{Re}(z)\,dz$ from $0$ to $1 + i$ along (a) the segment, (b) the path $0 \to 1 \to 1 + i$.
steps: (b) First leg $z = t$: $\int_0^1 t\,dt = \frac{1}{2}$. Second leg $z = 1 + it$: $\int_0^1 1 \cdot i\,dt = i$. Total $\frac{1}{2} + i$.
Different answers: $\operatorname{Re} z$ is not analytic, so it has no antiderivative and the path matters.

blocks.html: When does an analytic $f$ have an antiderivative? On a disk, always; more generally on any region without holes (a simply connected region), as Cauchy's theorem in the next lesson will show. The trouble with $\frac{1}{z}$ is the hole at $0$: on a region that surrounds the origin, no antiderivative exists.

Using $\operatorname{Log} z$ around a loop that circles $0$. It is tempting to write $\oint \frac{dz}{z} = \operatorname{Log}(\text{end}) - \operatorname{Log}(\text{start}) = 0$, since the end and the start are the same point. But $\operatorname{Log}$ is not analytic (not even continuous) on its cut, and the loop crosses the cut, where $\operatorname{Log}$ jumps by $2\pi i$. That jump is exactly the true answer: $2\pi i$. An antiderivative only counts if it is analytic along the whole path.

blocks.html: When $f$ has an antiderivative, closed integrals vanish. Cauchy's theorem says much more: analyticity alone is enough, with no antiderivative in sight, as long as $f$ is analytic inside the contour too. The proof joins Green's theorem with the Cauchy–Riemann equations, and the result is the backbone of the rest of the course.

Cauchy's theorem. If $f$ is analytic on and inside a simple closed contour $C$, then $$\oint_C f(z)\,dz = 0.$$ "Inside" matters: one point inside $C$ where $f$ is not analytic (such as $0$ for $\frac{1}{z}$) can make the integral nonzero.

Write $f = u + iv$ and $dz = dx + i\,dy$. Then $f\,dz = (u\,dx - v\,dy) + i(v\,dx + u\,dy)$. Apply Green's theorem, $\oint P\,dx + Q\,dy = \iint (Q_x - P_y)\,dA$, to each part (assuming continuous partials):
      $$\oint_C f\,dz = \iint_D (-v_x - u_y)\,dA + i\iint_D (u_x - v_y)\,dA.$$
      Both integrands are $0$ by the Cauchy–Riemann equations $u_y = -v_x$ and $u_x = v_y$. (Goursat later showed the theorem holds without assuming continuous partials.)

blocks.name: cplx-contour
blocks.cap: $f(z) = \frac{1}{z - 2}$ is analytic everywhere except at $2$. Drag the circle around: the integral is $0$ while $2$ stays outside, and jumps to $2\pi i$ the moment $2$ is inside.

blocks.title: An entire integrand
steps: $e^{z^2}\cos z$ is entire: analytic on and inside every contour.
By Cauchy's theorem, the integral is $0$. No parametrization needed (and none would be easy).

blocks.title: A singular point outside
steps: The only point where the integrand fails to be analytic is $z = 3$.
$|3| = 3 > 1$, so it lies outside the circle; the integrand is analytic on and inside $C$.

blocks.title: Counting the bad points
blocks.q: Which points where $f(z) = \dfrac{1}{(z^2 + 4)(z - 3)}$ is not analytic lie inside $|z - i| = 2$?
steps: Distances from $i$: $|2i - i| = 1$, $|-2i - i| = 3$, $|3 - i| = \sqrt{10}$. Only $2i$ is within $2$.
So Cauchy's theorem does not apply here; the integral is not automatically $0$ (later: it is $2\pi i$ times a residue at $2i$).

items: List the points where $f$ is not analytic (zeros of denominators, cuts of logarithms, anywhere $\overline{z}$ or $|z|$ appears).
Check which of them lie inside or on $C$.
If none does, the integral is $0$. If some do, the residue methods later in the course compute it.

blocks.html: Applying the theorem with a bad point inside. $\frac{1}{z}$ is analytic on the circle $|z| = 1$, yet $\oint_{|z| = 1}\frac{dz}{z} = 2\pi i$, because $0$ is inside. The hypothesis is "analytic on and inside $C$". Before writing $0$, list the points where $f$ is not analytic and check each one: inside or outside? Also check that $f$ is analytic at all; $\oint_{|z| = 2}\overline{z}\,dz = 8\pi i$, since $\overline{z}$ is not analytic anywhere.

blocks.html: Cauchy's theorem says integrals vanish when nothing bad is inside. When something bad is inside, the same theorem still helps: it lets us slide and shrink the contour freely, as long as we never drag it across a point where $f$ fails to be analytic. Then any contour around a point can be replaced by a tiny circle around it, where the integral is easy.

If $C_1$ can be deformed continuously into $C_2$ through a region where $f$ is analytic, then $\oint_{C_1} f\,dz = \oint_{C_2} f\,dz$. In particular, for any simple closed contour $C$ traced counterclockwise with $a$ inside,
      $$\oint_C \frac{dz}{(z - a)^n} = \begin{cases} 2\pi i, & n = 1, \\ 0, & n = 2, 3, \ldots \end{cases}$$
      and if $a$ is outside $C$, the integral is $0$ for every $n$.

Take a big contour $C$ and a small circle $c$ around $a$, both counterclockwise. Cut the ring between them with two close parallel slits; the boundary of the slit ring is a single closed contour (along $C$, in along one slit, around $c$ clockwise, out along the other slit), and $f$ is analytic inside it. By Cauchy's theorem its integral is $0$. The two slits cancel (same path, opposite directions), leaving $\oint_C f\,dz - \oint_c f\,dz = 0$. For $(z - a)^{-n}$ on the small circle, the circle computation gives $2\pi i$ for $n = 1$ and $0$ otherwise.

blocks.name: cplx-contour
blocks.cap: $f(z) = \frac{1}{z^2} + \frac{1}{z - 1}$ around a rectangle. Drag its corners: the value is $2\pi i$ when it encloses $1$ (whatever it does with $0$, since $\frac{1}{z^2}$ contributes nothing), and $0$ when it encloses neither.

blocks.title: A square instead of a circle
blocks.q: Compute $\displaystyle\oint_C \frac{5\,dz}{z - i}$, where $C$ is the square with corners $\pm 2 \pm 2i$, counterclockwise.
steps: The only bad point is $i$, inside the square.
Shrink the square to a small circle around $i$ without crossing $i$: the integral of $\frac{1}{z - i}$ is $2\pi i$.

blocks.title: A square power
steps: $-1$ is inside, but the power is $2$.
$\frac{1}{(z + 1)^2}$ has the antiderivative $-\frac{1}{z + 1}$ away from $-1$, so the integral is $0$.

blocks.title: Partial fractions
steps: On $|z| = 2$ only $0$ is inside: $\frac{1}{3}(0 - 2\pi i) = -\frac{2\pi i}{3}$.
On $|z| = 4$ both are inside: $\frac{1}{3}(2\pi i - 2\pi i) = 0$.

blocks.html: Expecting $\oint \frac{dz}{(z - a)^2}$ to be $2\pi i$ like the case $n = 1$. Only the power $-1$ survives a trip around $a$. Every other power has an antiderivative $\frac{(z - a)^{1 - n}}{1 - n}$ that is single-valued away from $a$, so its closed integrals are $0$. Check by parametrizing: $\int_0^{2\pi} ir^{1 - n}e^{i(1 - n)t}\,dt$ is $0$ unless $n = 1$.

blocks.html: Here is the most surprising fact in the course: the values of an analytic function on a closed curve determine its values everywhere inside. It follows from deforming the contour down to a tiny circle around the point.

Cauchy's integral formula. If $f$ is analytic on and inside a simple closed contour $C$ (counterclockwise) and $a$ is inside $C$, then $$f(a) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_C \frac{f(z)}{z - a}\,dz, \qquad\text{that is,}\qquad \oint_C \frac{f(z)}{z - a}\,dz = 2\pi i\,f(a).$$ If $a$ is outside $C$, the integral is $0$ (Cauchy's theorem).

The integrand is analytic except at $a$, so we may replace $C$ by a small circle $|z - a| = \varepsilon$. Split $\frac{f(z)}{z - a} = \frac{f(a)}{z - a} + \frac{f(z) - f(a)}{z - a}$. The first piece integrates to $2\pi i\,f(a)$. The second piece stays bounded near $a$ (its limit is $f'(a)$), say by $M$, so by the ML inequality its integral is at most $M \cdot 2\pi\varepsilon$, which tends to $0$. Since the integral does not depend on $\varepsilon$, it equals $2\pi i\,f(a)$ exactly.

blocks.name: cplx-contour
blocks.cap: $\frac{e^z}{z - 1}$ around a circle: while $1$ is inside, the integral is $2\pi i\,e^{1} \approx 17.08i$ for every circle you choose. The residue label shows $e \approx 2.718$, the value $f(1)$.

blocks.title: An exponential
steps: $f(z) = e^z$ is entire, and $a = 1$ is inside $|z| = 2$.

blocks.title: A polynomial at a complex point
steps: $a = i$ is the center, so it is inside; $f(z) = z^2 + 3$ is entire.

blocks.title: Factoring the denominator first
steps: $z^2 + 1 = (z - i)(z + i)$. Only $i$ is inside (the point $-i$ is $2$ away from the center).
Write the integrand as $\frac{g(z)}{z - i}$ with $g(z) = \frac{z}{z + i}$, analytic inside the circle.

blocks.html: The formula has striking consequences. An analytic function is completely determined inside a circle by its values on the circle: if two analytic functions agree on $C$, they agree inside. With a circle centered at $a$, it says $f(a)$ is the average of $f$ around the circle, the mean value property behind the maximum modulus principle. And in practice it evaluates integrals of the form $\oint\frac{f(z)}{z - a}dz$ by a single substitution.

items: Find the point $a$ where the denominator vanishes, and check that it is inside $C$.
Put everything else into $f(z)$ and check that $f$ is analytic on and inside $C$.
The integral is $2\pi i\,f(a)$.

blocks.html: Forgetting $2\pi i$, or using the formula with $a$ outside. The formula is $\oint \frac{f(z)}{z - a}dz = 2\pi i\,f(a)$, not $f(a)$; the $f(a)$ version needs the factor $\frac{1}{2\pi i}$ in front. And it only applies when $a$ is inside $C$: for $\oint_{|z| = 1}\frac{e^z}{z - 3}dz$ the answer is $0$, not $2\pi i e^3$. Check the location of $a$ first, every time.

blocks.html: Cauchy's formula writes $f(a)$ as an integral in which $a$ appears only in the simple factor $\frac{1}{z - a}$. Differentiating under the integral sign with respect to $a$ is then easy, and it gives formulas for every derivative. As a consequence, an analytic function automatically has derivatives of all orders.

If $f$ is analytic on and inside $C$ and $a$ is inside $C$, then for $n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$ $$f^{(n)}(a) = \frac{n!}{2\pi i}\oint_C \frac{f(z)}{(z - a)^{n + 1}}\,dz, \qquad\text{that is,}\qquad \oint_C \frac{f(z)}{(z - a)^{n + 1}}\,dz = \frac{2\pi i}{n!}f^{(n)}(a).$$ The power in the denominator is one more than the order of the derivative.

Differentiate $f(a) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint \frac{f(z)}{z - a}dz$ with respect to $a$: $\frac{d}{da}(z - a)^{-1} = (z - a)^{-2}$, then $2(z - a)^{-3}$, then $3!\,(z - a)^{-4}$, and so on, giving $n!\,(z - a)^{-(n + 1)}$ after $n$ steps. Moving the derivative inside the integral is justified because the integrand is a smooth function of $a$ on the contour. Since the right side exists for every $n$, so does $f^{(n)}(a)$: one complex derivative on an open set brings all the others with it.

blocks.name: cplx-contour
blocks.cap: $\frac{e^{2z}}{(z - 1)^3}$: a pole of order 3 at $1$. The integral is $\frac{2\pi i}{2!}\cdot(e^{2z})''\big|_{z = 1} = 4\pi e^2\,i \approx 92.85i$.

$n$
Integral equals
blocks.cap: The first few cases of $\oint_C \frac{f(z)}{(z - a)^{n + 1}}dz = \frac{2\pi i}{n!}f^{(n)}(a)$.

blocks.html: Compare with real calculus, where $f(x) = x|x|$ has a first derivative but no second at $0$. Nothing like that can happen for analytic functions: once $f'$ exists on an open set, $f''$, $f'''$ and all the rest exist there too, and each is analytic.

blocks.title: A product on top
steps: $n = 1$ with $f(z) = ze^z$ and $a = 2$, inside the circle.

blocks.html: The same formula gives Taylor coefficients: the coefficient of $(z - a)^n$ in the Taylor series of $f$ is $\frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!} = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_C\frac{f(z)}{(z - a)^{n + 1}}dz$. So integrals of this kind are really asking for one Taylor coefficient, which is often the quickest way to compute them.

Taking the power $n + 1$ as the order of the derivative, or dropping $n!$. In $\oint \frac{f(z)}{(z - a)^4}dz$ the derivative is $f'''$ (order $3$, not $4$), and the factor is $\frac{2\pi i}{3!} = \frac{\pi i}{3}$. A quick check with $f(z) = (z - a)^3$: the integrand is $\frac{1}{z - a}$, the integral is $2\pi i$, and the formula gives $\frac{2\pi i}{3!}\cdot 3! = 2\pi i$. Only the right $n$ and the $n!$ make that work.

blocks.html: Cauchy's formula for derivatives, combined with the ML inequality, limits how fast an analytic function can change. For a function analytic on the whole plane, the limit becomes so strong that a bounded one cannot change at all. One consequence finishes a promise from Algebra 2: every polynomial has a complex root.

Cauchy's estimate. If $f$ is analytic on and inside $|z - a| = R$ and $|f| \le M$ on that circle, then $|f^{(n)}(a)| \le \dfrac{n!\,M}{R^n}$.
Liouville's theorem. A bounded entire function is constant.
Fundamental theorem of algebra. Every nonconstant polynomial has a complex zero, so a polynomial of degree $n$ has exactly $n$ zeros counted with multiplicity.

By the derivative formula and ML: $|f^{(n)}(a)| = \frac{n!}{2\pi}\left|\oint \frac{f(z)}{(z - a)^{n + 1}}dz\right| \le \frac{n!}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{M}{R^{n + 1}}\cdot 2\pi R = \frac{n!M}{R^n}$. If $f$ is entire with $|f| \le M$ everywhere, take $n = 1$ and let $R \to \infty$: $|f'(a)| \le \frac{M}{R} \to 0$, so $f' = 0$ everywhere and $f$ is constant. For a polynomial $p$ with no zero, $\frac{1}{p}$ would be entire and tend to $0$ as $|z| \to \infty$, hence bounded, hence constant, which is impossible unless $p$ is constant. Dividing out one root at a time gives all $n$.

blocks.name: cplx-domaincolor
blocks.cap: $\sin z$ is entire, and bounded on the real axis (blue graph), but up the imaginary axis (orange) it grows like $\frac{1}{2}e^{|y|}$. It had to: by Liouville, a bounded entire function is constant.

blocks.title: A bounded entire function
blocks.q: An entire function satisfies $|f(z)| \le 7$ for all $z$ and $f(2) = 3 - i$. Find $f(5i)$.
steps: $f$ is entire and bounded, so it is constant.

blocks.title: Cauchy's estimate
blocks.q: $f$ is analytic on and inside $|z| = 3$ with $|f| \le 9$ there. How large can $|f''(0)|$ be?
steps: The bound is reached by $f(z) = z^2$, which has $|f| = 9$ on the circle and $f''(0) = 2$.

blocks.title: Growth forces a polynomial
blocks.q: An entire function has $|f(z)| \le 3|z|^2 + 5$ for all $z$. What can you say about $f'''(0)$?
steps: As $R \to \infty$ the right side tends to $0$, so $f'''(0) = 0$; the same works for every higher derivative at every point.
So $f$ is a polynomial of degree at most $2$.

blocks.html: Offering $\sin z$ (or $\cos z$, or $e^{iz}$) as a bounded entire function. They are bounded on the real line, but not on the plane: $|\sin(iy)| = |\sinh y|$ and $|e^{iz}| = e^{-y}$ both blow up. Liouville's theorem has no exceptions. When a function seems to break it, check whether it is really entire (no poles anywhere) and really bounded on all of $\mathbb{C}$, especially along the imaginary axis.

blocks.html: Take Cauchy's formula on a circle centered at $a$: it says $f(a)$ is the average of $f$ over the circle. An average can never be bigger than every value it averages, and that simple observation controls where $|f|$ can be largest.

Maximum modulus principle. If $f$ is analytic and not constant on a bounded region $D$ and continuous on its closure, then $|f|$ reaches its maximum on the boundary of $D$, never at an interior point.
If moreover $f$ has no zeros in $D$, the minimum of $|f|$ is on the boundary too (apply the principle to $\frac{1}{f}$).

With $z = a + re^{it}$ in Cauchy's formula, $dz = ire^{it}dt$ and $z - a = re^{it}$, so $f(a) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f(a + re^{it})\,dt$: the mean value property. Suppose $|f|$ had its largest value $M$ at an interior point $a$. Then $M = |f(a)| \le \frac{1}{2\pi}\int |f(a + re^{it})|\,dt \le M$, so equality holds and $|f| = M$ on every small circle around $a$. Then $|f|$ is constant near $a$, which (by the Cauchy–Riemann equations) forces $f$ to be constant.

blocks.name: cplx-domaincolor
blocks.cap: $f(z) = z^2 + z + 1$ on the closed unit disk: the largest $|f|$ is marked, on the edge at $z = 1$ where $|f| = 3$. Inside the disk the brightness rings never reach that level.

blocks.title: A linear function
blocks.q: Find the maximum of $|z + 3 - 4i|$ on $|z| \le 2$ and where it happens.
steps: The maximum is on the circle $|z| = 2$.
$|z + (3 - 4i)| \le |z| + |3 - 4i| = 2 + 5 = 7$, with equality when $z$ points the same way as $3 - 4i$.

blocks.title: An exponential
steps: On the closed disk, $-y$ is largest at $z = -i$, where $-y = 1$.
The maximum is $e$, at $z = -i$, on the boundary.

blocks.title: A minimum
steps: $z + 3$ has its only zero at $-3$, outside the disk, so the minimum is on the boundary.

blocks.html: The same idea works for the real part: a harmonic function $u$ (such as $\operatorname{Re} f$) takes its maximum and minimum over a closed bounded region on the boundary. In heat flow this says the steady temperature inside a plate is never hotter than the hottest point of its edge.

Hunting for the maximum at a critical point inside. In multivariable calculus you set the gradient to zero and test interior points. For $|f|$ with $f$ analytic, interior critical points are never maxima (and $f'(z_0) = 0$ is a different thing altogether). Go straight to the boundary: parametrize it, or use the triangle inequality and check when equality holds.

blocks.html: Power series in Calculus 2 converged on an interval centered at $a$. With complex $z$, the interval becomes a disk, a region you already know how to read. The complex picture also explains something that the real line keeps hidden: why the radius is what it is.

A power series $\sum_{n \ge 0} c_n(z - a)^n$ has a radius of convergence $R$ (with $0 \le R \le \infty$): it converges absolutely for $|z - a| < R$ and diverges for $|z - a| > R$ (on the circle itself anything can happen). The ratio test finds it: if $\left|\frac{c_{n + 1}}{c_n}\right| \to \lambda$, then $R = \frac{1}{\lambda}$ (with $R = \infty$ when $\lambda = 0$). Inside its disk the sum is analytic, and it can be differentiated term by term.

Compare with a geometric series. If the series converges at some $z_1$, its terms are bounded: $|c_n(z_1 - a)^n| \le K$. Then for $|z - a| < |z_1 - a|$,
      $$|c_n(z - a)^n| \le K\left|\frac{z - a}{z_1 - a}\right|^n,$$
      a convergent geometric series. So convergence at one point gives convergence on the whole disk through that point, and the set of convergence is a disk (plus perhaps some boundary points). The ratio test is this same comparison done with $\frac{|c_{n + 1}||z - a|}{|c_n|} \to \lambda|z - a| < 1$.

blocks.name: cplx-series
blocks.cap: The Maclaurin series of $\frac{1}{1 + z^2} = 1 - z^2 + z^4 - \cdots$: dark where the partial sum is accurate. The disk stops at radius $1$ because of the singular points $\pm i$. The real graph (below) is perfectly smooth, yet the partial sums fail past $|x| = 1$: the cause is off the real line.

blocks.title: A geometric series
blocks.q: Find the radius of convergence of $\displaystyle\sum_{n \ge 0}\frac{z^n}{(3 + 4i)^n}$.
steps: It is geometric with ratio $\frac{z}{3 + 4i}$, convergent exactly when $\left|\frac{z}{3 + 4i}\right| < 1$.

blocks.title: The ratio test
blocks.q: Find the radius of convergence of $\displaystyle\sum_{n \ge 1}\frac{n^2z^n}{2^n}$, and of $\displaystyle\sum_{n \ge 0}\frac{z^n}{n!}$.
steps: First: $\left|\frac{c_{n + 1}}{c_n}\right| = \frac{(n + 1)^2}{n^2}\cdot\frac{1}{2} \to \frac{1}{2}$, so $R = 2$. The polynomial factor $n^2$ does not change the radius.
Second: $\frac{n!}{(n + 1)!} = \frac{1}{n + 1} \to 0$, so $R = \infty$: the exponential series converges everywhere.

blocks.title: The radius from the singular points
blocks.q: What is the radius of convergence of the Maclaurin series of $\dfrac{1}{z^2 - 2z + 5}$?
steps: Both are at distance $|1 \pm 2i| = \sqrt{5}$ from the center $0$.
$R = \sqrt{5}$. (The next lesson proves that the radius reaches exactly to the nearest singular point.)

blocks.html: Expecting the Maclaurin series of $\frac{1}{1 + x^2}$ to converge for every real $x$. The function is smooth on the whole real line, so this seems natural. But the series $1 - x^2 + x^4 - \cdots$ diverges for $|x| \ge 1$. The reason is complex: at $z = \pm i$ the function blows up, and the disk of convergence cannot reach past them. To find a radius, look for singular points in the whole complex plane, not only on the real line.

blocks.html: In real calculus, a function with derivatives of every order can still fail to equal its Taylor series. Complex analysis has no such gap. Cauchy's formula turns into a power series directly, and the disk where it converges is as large as it could possibly be.

If $f$ is analytic on the disk $|z - a| < R$, then on that whole disk
      $$f(z) = \sum_{n \ge 0}\frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}(z - a)^n.$$
      So the radius of convergence of the Taylor series at $a$ is at least the distance from $a$ to the nearest point where $f$ fails to be analytic (and for functions like rational ones, exactly that distance).

Fix $z$ in the disk and take a circle $C$ around $a$ that encloses $z$. In Cauchy's formula $f(z) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_C\frac{f(w)}{w - z}dw$, expand the kernel as a geometric series:
      $$\frac{1}{w - z} = \frac{1}{(w - a) - (z - a)} = \sum_{n \ge 0}\frac{(z - a)^n}{(w - a)^{n + 1}}, \qquad \text{valid since } |z - a| < |w - a|.$$
      Integrate term by term: the coefficient of $(z - a)^n$ is $\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_C\frac{f(w)}{(w - a)^{n + 1}}dw = \frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}$. The only requirement was a circle inside the domain, so the series works out to the nearest bad point.

blocks.name: cplx-series
blocks.cap: The Taylor series of $\frac{1}{1 - z}$ about $a = i$: its disk reaches to the singular point $1$, so the radius is $|1 - i| = \sqrt{2}$, not $1$. Drag the center and watch the disk follow the distance to $1$.

blocks.title: A new center
blocks.q: Find the Taylor series of $\dfrac{1}{1 - z}$ about $a = i$ and its radius of convergence.
steps: Write $1 - z = (1 - i) - (z - i)$, so $\frac{1}{1 - z} = \frac{1}{1 - i}\cdot\frac{1}{1 - \frac{z - i}{1 - i}}$.
Geometric series: $\frac{1}{1 - z} = \sum_{n \ge 0}\frac{(z - i)^n}{(1 - i)^{n + 1}}$, valid for $|z - i| < |1 - i|$.
Radius $\sqrt{2}$: the distance from $i$ to the singular point $1$.

blocks.title: A coefficient
blocks.q: Find the coefficient of $z^3$ in the Maclaurin series of $e^{(1 + i)z}$.
steps: $e^w = \sum\frac{w^n}{n!}$ with $w = (1 + i)z$; the $z^3$ term is $\frac{(1 + i)^3}{3!}z^3$.

blocks.title: Radius from the nearest singular point
blocks.q: Find the radius of convergence of the Taylor series of $\dfrac{e^z}{z^2 + 4}$ about $a = 1$.
steps: $e^z$ is entire; the bad points are $\pm 2i$.

items: $e^z = \sum \frac{z^n}{n!}$, $\sin z = \sum \frac{(-1)^nz^{2n + 1}}{(2n + 1)!}$, $\cos z = \sum \frac{(-1)^nz^{2n}}{(2n)!}$: valid for every $z$.
$\frac{1}{1 - z} = \sum z^n$: valid for $|z| < 1$, the distance from $0$ to the pole at $1$.
Substituting into these (for example $z^2$ or $-z$ for $z$) gives most series you need, valid on the corresponding region.

blocks.html: Reusing a known series without changing the center. $\frac{1}{1 - z} = \sum z^n$ is the series about $0$, valid for $|z| < 1$. About $a = i$ you need powers of $z - i$, and the radius changes to $|1 - i| = \sqrt{2}$. Check: the center of a Taylor series is wherever the powers $(z - a)^n$ vanish, and its radius is the distance from that center to the nearest singular point.

blocks.html: A Taylor series lives on a disk, and stops at the first singular point. Around a singular point, or in a ring between two of them, we need negative powers too. Expanding with the geometric series in the right variable is almost always the tool, as in the previous lesson.

If $f$ is analytic on an annulus $r < |z - a| < R$, then on that annulus
      $$f(z) = \sum_{n = -\infty}^{\infty} c_n(z - a)^n, \qquad c_n = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_C\frac{f(w)}{(w - a)^{n + 1}}\,dw,$$
      for any circle $C$ in the annulus. The series is unique for that annulus, but a different annulus (around the same center) gets a different series. The basic rule: $\frac{1}{z - c} = -\frac{1}{c}\sum_{n \ge 0}\left(\frac{z}{c}\right)^n$ where $|z| < |c|$, and $\frac{1}{z - c} = \frac{1}{z}\sum_{n \ge 0}\left(\frac{c}{z}\right)^n$ where $|z| > |c|$.

For the two expansions of $\frac{1}{z - c}$, factor out whichever of $z$ and $c$ is bigger, so the ratio inside the geometric series has modulus less than 1: $\frac{1}{z - c} = \frac{-1}{c}\cdot\frac{1}{1 - z/c}$ or $\frac{1}{z}\cdot\frac{1}{1 - c/z}$. For a general $f$, Cauchy's formula on the boundary of the annulus splits $f$ into a piece analytic inside the outer circle (a Taylor series in $z - a$) and a piece analytic outside the inner circle (a series in $\frac{1}{z - a}$).

blocks.name: cplx-series
blocks.cap: $\frac{1}{z(z - 1)}$ has two rings around $0$: $0 < |z| < 1$ and $|z| > 1$. Switch between them: each has its own Laurent series, accurate (dark) only on its own ring.

blocks.title: A middle ring
blocks.q: Find the coefficient of $z^{-1}$ and of $z^{0}$ for $f(z) = \dfrac{1}{(z - 1)(z - 2)}$ on $1 < |z| < 2$.

blocks.title: An essential singularity
blocks.q: Find the Laurent series of $z^2e^{1/z}$ on $|z| > 0$ and its coefficient of $z^{-1}$.
steps: The coefficient of $z^{-1}$ is $\frac{1}{6}$; infinitely many negative powers appear.

items: Split the function into partial fractions $\frac{A}{z - c}$.
For each pole $c$, compare $|c|$ with the ring: if the ring lies inside $|z| < |c|$, expand in powers of $\frac{z}{c}$; if outside, in powers of $\frac{c}{z}$.
Add the expansions and collect the coefficient you need.

blocks.html: Using the wrong geometric series for the ring. On $|z| > 1$, writing $\frac{1}{z - 1} = -\sum z^n$ is wrong: that series diverges there. The ratio must be small: on $|z| > 1$ use powers of $\frac{1}{z}$. A quick check: plug in a point of the ring (such as $z = 2$ for $|z| > 1$) and ask whether the terms of your series shrink.
