blocks.html: A point where $f$ is not analytic, but analytic on a small punctured disk around it, is an isolated singularity. Its Laurent series on that punctured disk sorts it into one of three kinds, and the kind decides how integrals around it behave.

Let $f(z) = \sum c_n(z - a)^n$ on $0 < |z - a| < r$.
• Removable: no negative powers. $f$ has a finite limit at $a$ and becomes analytic once $f(a)$ is defined as that limit. Example: $\frac{\sin z}{z}$ at $0$.
• Pole of order $m$: the negative powers stop at $(z - a)^{-m}$. Equivalently $f = \frac{g(z)}{(z - a)^m}$ with $g$ analytic and $g(a) \ne 0$; then $|f| \to \infty$. Example: $\frac{1}{z^2(z - 1)}$ has a pole of order 2 at $0$.
• Essential: infinitely many negative powers. Example: $e^{1/z}$ at $0$, which comes arbitrarily close to every complex value near $0$.
A zero of order $m$ means $f = (z - a)^mg(z)$ with $g(a) \ne 0$; a zero of order $m$ on the bottom of a quotient gives a pole of order $m$.

The three cases cover everything: the negative part of the Laurent series either is empty, stops, or goes on forever. If it stops at $(z - a)^{-m}$, multiplying by $(z - a)^m$ leaves an ordinary power series $g$ with $g(a) = c_{-m} 
e 0$. For a quotient $ rac{h}{k}$ where $h(a) 
e 0$ and $k$ has a zero of order $m$, write $k = (z - a)^m q(z)$ with $q(a) 
e 0$; then $ rac{h}{k} =  rac{h/q}{(z - a)^m}$, a pole of order $m$. If $h$ also vanishes at $a$, subtract its order from $m$.

blocks.name: cplx-domaincolor
blocks.cap: $e^{1/z}$ near $0$: every color appears in every neighborhood of $0$, in endlessly shrinking loops. A pole would show the colors going around a fixed number of times; this is an essential singularity.

blocks.title: Cancelling zeros
blocks.q: Classify the singularity at $0$ of $\dfrac{1 - \cos z}{z^4}$.

blocks.title: Removable
blocks.q: Classify the singularity of $\dfrac{\sin z}{z}$ at $0$.
steps: Removable, with limit $1$; defining the value at $0$ to be $1$ makes the function entire.

blocks.html: Misreading the kind. $\frac{\sin z}{z}$ looks like it has a pole at $0$ because of the $z$ in the denominator, but the top vanishes there too: it is removable. And $e^{1/z}$ is not a pole: along the positive real axis it blows up, but along the negative real axis it tends to $0$, so it is not true that $|f| \to \infty$. Check with the Laurent series: count the negative powers.

blocks.html: Integrate a Laurent series term by term around a small circle centered at an isolated singularity $a$: every power $(z - a)^n$ gives $0$ except $n = -1$, which gives $2\pi i$. So only one coefficient matters for integrals, and it gets a name.

The residue of $f$ at an isolated singularity $a$ is the coefficient $c_{-1}$ of $(z - a)^{-1}$ in the Laurent series about $a$; then $\oint_{|z - a| = \varepsilon} f\,dz = 2\pi i\operatorname{Res}(f, a)$. At a simple pole: $$\operatorname{Res}(f, a) = \lim_{z \to a}(z - a)f(z), \qquad\text{and if } f = \frac{g}{h} \text{ with } g(a) \ne 0,\ h(a) = 0,\ h'(a) \ne 0: \quad \operatorname{Res}(f, a) = \frac{g(a)}{h'(a)}.$$

At a simple pole, $f = \frac{c_{-1}}{z - a} + c_0 + c_1(z - a) + \cdots$, so $(z - a)f(z) = c_{-1} + c_0(z - a) + \cdots \to c_{-1}$. For $f = \frac{g}{h}$: $(z - a)\frac{g(z)}{h(z)} = \frac{g(z)}{\frac{h(z) - h(a)}{z - a}} \to \frac{g(a)}{h'(a)}$, using $h(a) = 0$ and the definition of the derivative. The condition $h'(a) \ne 0$ is what makes the zero of $h$ (and so the pole) simple.

blocks.name: cplx-contour
blocks.cap: A small circle around the simple pole at $i$ of $\frac{z + 2}{z^2 + 1}$. The integral divided by $2\pi i$ is the residue $\frac{i + 2}{2i} = \frac{1}{2} - i$. Move the circle to $-i$ to see the other residue.

blocks.title: Cover-up
steps: $z = 1$ is a simple pole. Multiply by $z - 1$: $\frac{1}{z + 2}$.

blocks.title: Using $g/h'$
blocks.q: Find the residue of $\dfrac{z + 2}{z^2 + 1}$ at $z = i$.
steps: $g(z) = z + 2$, $h(z) = z^2 + 1$, $h'(z) = 2z$; $h'(i) = 2i \ne 0$, so the pole is simple.

blocks.title: A trigonometric quotient
blocks.q: Find the residue of $\cot z$ at $z = \pi$, and of $\dfrac{1}{e^z - 1}$ at $z = 2\pi i$.
steps: $\cot z = \frac{\cos z}{\sin z}$, and $\sin$ has a simple zero at $\pi$ with $\sin'(\pi) = \cos\pi$: residue $\frac{\cos\pi}{\cos\pi} = 1$.
$h(z) = e^z - 1$ has $h'(2\pi i) = e^{2\pi i} = 1$: residue $\frac{1}{1} = 1$.

items: Simple pole, factored denominator: cover up the factor $(z - a)$ and evaluate the rest at $a$.
Simple pole of $\frac{g}{h}$ with $h(a) = 0$, $h'(a) \ne 0$: use $\frac{g(a)}{h'(a)}$. This is the quickest for $\tan$, $\cot$, $\frac{1}{e^z - 1}$ and denominators like $z^4 - 1$.
Any isolated singularity: read $c_{-1}$ from the Laurent series (the only option at an essential singularity).

blocks.html: A removable singularity has residue $0$, and so does any point where $f$ is analytic. The residue at a pole can be $0$ too: $\frac{1}{z^2}$ has a double pole at $0$ with residue $0$, which is why $\oint\frac{dz}{z^2} = 0$.
Why "residue"? It is what is left over: after integrating around a small circle, every term of the Laurent series disappears except $c_{-1}$.

Using $\frac{g(a)}{h'(a)}$ at a pole that is not simple. For $\frac{1}{z^2(z - 1)}$ at $0$, $h(z) = z^3 - z^2$ has $h'(0) = 0$: the formula would divide by zero, and the pole is double. Check the order first (does $h'(a) \ne 0$? is the factor $(z - a)$ to the first power?). For higher-order poles, use the derivative formula of the next lesson.

MIT OpenCourseWare 18.04, Complex Variables with Applications (Spring 2018), course notes: residue theorem

blocks.html: At a simple pole, multiplying by $z - a$ exposes the residue. At a pole of order $m$, multiply by $(z - a)^m$ instead: the residue is then hidden one step deeper, as a Taylor coefficient that a few derivatives can reach.

If $f$ has a pole of order $m$ at $a$, then
      $$\operatorname{Res}(f, a) = \frac{1}{(m - 1)!}\lim_{z \to a}\frac{d^{m - 1}}{dz^{m - 1}}\Big[(z - a)^mf(z)\Big].$$
      Often a series expansion is faster: the residue is the coefficient of $(z - a)^{m - 1}$ in the Taylor series of $(z - a)^mf(z)$.

With $f = \frac{c_{-m}}{(z - a)^m} + \cdots + \frac{c_{-1}}{z - a} + c_0 + \cdots$, the function $g(z) = (z - a)^mf(z) = c_{-m} + \cdots + c_{-1}(z - a)^{m - 1} + c_0(z - a)^m + \cdots$ is analytic at $a$. Its Taylor coefficient of $(z - a)^{m - 1}$ is $c_{-1}$, and Taylor's formula says that coefficient equals $\frac{g^{(m - 1)}(a)}{(m - 1)!}$.

blocks.name: cplx-contour
blocks.cap: $\frac{e^z}{z^3}$ has a pole of order 3 at $0$; its residue is $\frac{1}{2!}(e^z)''\big|_{0} = \frac{1}{2}$, so the integral is $\pi i$.

blocks.title: An exponential over a power
steps: Series check: the $z^2$ coefficient of $e^{2z}$ is $\frac{2^2}{2!} = 2$.

blocks.title: A double pole
steps: Differentiate once: $-\frac{1}{(z + 1)^2}$, and at $z = 1$ this is $-\frac{1}{4}$ (then divide by $1! = 1$).

blocks.title: A series is quicker
steps: The residue is $-\frac{1}{6}$. (The pole has order 3, not 4, because $\sin z$ vanishes at $0$.)

blocks.html: Which method to use? For a pole of order 2 the derivative formula is usually quickest: one derivative of $(z - a)^2f(z)$. For order 3 or more, or when the top is $\sin$, $\cos$ or $e^z$, expanding in a series and reading off one coefficient is often faster and less error-prone than taking several derivatives of a quotient.

blocks.title: A pole of order 2 at a complex point

blocks.html: A useful special case: if $f = \frac{g(z)}{(z - a)^m}$ with $g$ analytic at $a$, the residue is $\frac{g^{(m - 1)}(a)}{(m - 1)!}$, the coefficient of $(z - a)^{m - 1}$ in the Taylor series of $g$.

Forgetting $\frac{1}{(m - 1)!}$, or using the wrong order $m$. For $\frac{e^z}{z^4}$, $m = 4$ and the residue is $\frac{1}{3!}(e^z)'''(0) = \frac{1}{6}$, not $1$. And for $\frac{\sin z}{z^4}$ the order is $3$, since the top vanishes at $0$; using $m = 4$ still works (an overestimate of $m$ is harmless if you differentiate correctly), but using too small an $m$ gives nonsense. Check against the Laurent series when in doubt.

blocks.html: Deforming contours let us replace a big contour by small circles around each point inside where $f$ fails to be analytic. Each small circle contributes $2\pi i$ times a residue. Put together, that is the residue theorem, the main computing tool of the course.

Residue theorem. If $f$ is analytic on and inside a simple closed contour $C$ (counterclockwise) except at finitely many isolated singularities $a_1, \ldots, a_k$ inside $C$, then $$\oint_C f(z)\,dz = 2\pi i\sum_{j = 1}^{k}\operatorname{Res}(f, a_j).$$ Singularities outside $C$ do not count.

Draw a small circle $c_j$ around each $a_j$. Cutting slits from $C$ to each $c_j$, as in the deformation argument, shows that $\oint_C f\,dz = \sum_j \oint_{c_j} f\,dz$, because $f$ is analytic in the region between them. On $c_j$, integrate the Laurent series about $a_j$ term by term: only the $(z - a_j)^{-1}$ term survives, giving $2\pi i\operatorname{Res}(f, a_j)$.

blocks.name: cplx-contour
blocks.cap: Three simple poles at $0$, $1$ and $-2$. The circle encloses $0$ and $1$; the readout adds their residues. Drag the circle to enclose $-2$ as well: the sum of all three residues is $0$, so the integral becomes $0$.

blocks.title: With a double pole
steps: Inside: the double pole at $0$. Outside: $3$.

items: Find all singular points of $f$.
Decide which lie inside $C$ (compare distances from the center with the radius, or sketch).
Compute the residue at each inside point, using the simple-pole or higher-order formulas.
Multiply the sum by $2\pi i$.

blocks.html: The residue theorem contains the earlier results: with no singular points inside it is Cauchy's theorem, and for $\frac{f(z)}{z - a}$ the residue at $a$ is $f(a)$, giving Cauchy's integral formula. For a rational function whose bottom has degree at least two more than the top, the residues at all its poles add up to $0$, which can save work.
Orientation matters: a clockwise contour gives $-2\pi i$ times the sum of the residues inside.

Including residues of poles outside the contour. The theorem sums over the singularities inside $C$ only. Before computing any residue, list all singular points with their distances from the center of $C$ and cross out the ones outside. That also saves work: there is no need to compute residues you will not use.

blocks.html: Here is the first payoff of the residue theorem: real integrals of trigonometric expressions over a full turn, which are hard by real methods, become contour integrals around the unit circle.

For $\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi} R(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)\,d\theta$, put $z = e^{i\theta}$. As $\theta$ runs from $0$ to $2\pi$, $z$ goes once around $|z| = 1$, and
      $$\cos\theta = \frac{z + z^{-1}}{2}, \qquad \sin\theta = \frac{z - z^{-1}}{2i}, \qquad d\theta = \frac{dz}{iz}.$$
      The integral becomes $\oint_{|z| = 1}(\text{a rational function of } z)\,dz = 2\pi i\,\times$ (sum of the residues inside the unit circle). A standard result: for $a > |b|$,
      $$\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\theta}{a + b\cos\theta} = \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{a^2 - b^2}}.$$

The substitutions come from Euler's formula: $z + \frac{1}{z} = e^{i\theta} + e^{-i\theta} = 2\cos\theta$, and similarly for sine. From $z = e^{i\theta}$, $dz = ie^{i\theta}d\theta = iz\,d\theta$, so $d\theta = \frac{dz}{iz}$. For the standard result, $a + b\frac{z + z^{-1}}{2} = \frac{bz^2 + 2az + b}{2z}$, so the integrand becomes $\frac{2}{i(bz^2 + 2az + b)}$. The two roots of $bz^2 + 2az + b$ multiply to $1$; the one inside the unit circle is $z_1 = \frac{-a + \sqrt{a^2 - b^2}}{b}$, with residue $\frac{2}{ib(z_1 - z_2)} = \frac{1}{i\sqrt{a^2 - b^2}}$. Times $2\pi i$ gives the result.

blocks.name: cplx-contour
blocks.cap: $\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\theta}{5 + 3\cos\theta}$: as $\theta$ moves, $z = e^{i\theta}$ goes around the unit circle. The integrand in $z$ has poles at $-\frac{1}{3}$ (inside) and $-3$ (outside); only the inside one counts, and the numerical integral matches $2\pi i$ times its residue, $\frac{\pi}{2}$.

blocks.title: With sine
steps: The same method (or the same formula with $\sin$, since shifting $\theta$ by $\frac{\pi}{2}$ turns $\cos$ into $\sin$ over a full period) gives $\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{169 - 25}}$.

blocks.title: A double pole inside
steps: The integrand becomes $\frac{dz}{iz}\cdot\frac{4z^2}{(3z^2 + 10z + 3)^2} = \frac{4z\,dz}{9i(z + \frac{1}{3})^2(z + 3)^2}$, with a double pole at $-\frac{1}{3}$ inside.

items: Replace $\cos\theta$, $\sin\theta$ and $d\theta$ using $z = e^{i\theta}$, and simplify to one fraction in $z$.
Find the poles and keep those with $|z| < 1$.
Add their residues and multiply by $2\pi i$. The result must be real; if it is not, recheck the factor $\frac{1}{iz}$.

blocks.html: The method needs a full period $0$ to $2\pi$. For $\int_0^{\pi}$, use symmetry first (for example, an even function of $\cos\theta$ over $[0, \pi]$ is half of the integral over $[0, 2\pi]$).

Forgetting $d\theta = \frac{dz}{iz}$, or counting poles outside the circle. Leaving out the factor $\frac{1}{iz}$ changes the integrand and its poles, and the answer comes out wrong (often not even real). And of the two roots of $bz^2 + 2az + b$, only the one with modulus less than $1$ is inside; including both gives $0$. Check: the original integral is a real number, and positive when the integrand is positive.

blocks.html: Improper integrals over the whole real line, such as $\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{dx}{x^2 + 1}$, can be done with residues even when no antiderivative is in sight. The idea: close the real line into a loop with a large half circle, and use the ML inequality to show the half circle contributes nothing.

Let $f = \frac{P}{Q}$ with polynomials $P, Q$, $\deg Q \ge \deg P + 2$, and $Q$ never $0$ on the real line. Then $$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\,dx = 2\pi i\sum_{\operatorname{Im} a > 0}\operatorname{Res}\left(\frac{P}{Q}, a\right),$$ the sum over the poles in the upper half-plane only.

Let $C_R$ be the segment $[-R, R]$ followed by the upper half circle $\Gamma_R$ of radius $R$. For $R$ large, $C_R$ encloses every upper pole, so $\int_{-R}^{R} f\,dx + \int_{\Gamma_R} f\,dz = 2\pi i\sum\operatorname{Res}$. On $\Gamma_R$, $|f(z)| \le \frac{K}{R^2}$ for some constant $K$ (two degrees of decay), and the length is $\pi R$, so $\left|\int_{\Gamma_R}f\,dz\right| \le \frac{\pi K}{R} \to 0$. Letting $R \to \infty$ leaves the real integral equal to $2\pi i\sum\operatorname{Res}$.

blocks.name: cplx-contour
blocks.cap: For $\frac{1}{z^2 + 1}$ the half-disk encloses only $i$. Drag the handle outward: the arc's integral shrinks toward $0$ and the straight part approaches the whole real integral, $\pi$.

blocks.title: The basic case
steps: Poles at $\pm 2i$; only $2i$ is in the upper half-plane.

items: Check the conditions: no real zeros of $Q$, and $\deg Q \ge \deg P + 2$.
Find the zeros of $Q$ with positive imaginary part.
Add the residues of $\frac{P}{Q}$ there and multiply by $2\pi i$.

blocks.html: Why two degrees? With only one degree of decay, as in $\frac{x}{x^2 + 1}$, the arc's ML bound $\frac{\pi R \cdot R}{R^2 - 1}$ does not shrink, and in fact $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{x}{x^2 + 1}dx$ does not converge. The degree condition is what makes both the real integral and the arc argument work.

blocks.title: A shifted denominator
steps: The zeros of $x^2 + 2x + 5$ are $-1 \pm 2i$; only $-1 + 2i$ is in the upper half-plane.

blocks.html: Including the poles in the lower half-plane. The closed contour (segment plus upper half circle) does not surround the lower poles, so their residues do not belong in the sum. For $\frac{1}{x^2 + 4}$, adding the residue at $-2i$ would give $0$, an impossible value for the integral of a positive function. Quick check: a positive integrand must give a positive real answer.

blocks.html: Integrals like $\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{\cos x}{x^2 + 1}dx$ appear in Fourier analysis and in physics. The half-disk method handles them too, with one change: replace $\cos(ax)$ by the exponential $e^{iaz}$, which stays small in the upper half-plane.

For $a > 0$ and a rational $R(x)$ with no real poles that tends to $0$ at $\pm\infty$:
      $$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}R(x)e^{iax}\,dx = 2\pi i\sum_{\operatorname{Im} z_j > 0}\operatorname{Res}\left(R(z)e^{iaz}, z_j\right),$$
      and the cosine and sine integrals are its real and imaginary parts (for real $R$). For example, for $k, b > 0$,
      $$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\cos(kx)}{x^2 + b^2}\,dx = \frac{\pi e^{-kb}}{b}.$$

On the upper half-plane, $z = x + iy$ with $y \ge 0$, so $|e^{iaz}| = |e^{iax}e^{-ay}| = e^{-ay} \le 1$: the exponential does not grow, and when $\deg Q \ge \deg P + 2$ the ML bound kills the arc as before. (When $R$ decays only like $\frac{1}{x}$, a sharper estimate called Jordan's lemma still kills it.) For the example: the upper pole is $bi$, with residue $\frac{e^{ik(bi)}}{2bi} = \frac{e^{-kb}}{2bi}$, and $2\pi i$ times that is $\frac{\pi e^{-kb}}{b}$, a real number, which is the cosine integral (the sine part is $0$ by symmetry).

blocks.name: cplx-contour
blocks.cap: $\frac{e^{iz}}{z^2 + 1}$ around the half-disk: the arc's contribution fades as $R$ grows, and the total is $\frac{\pi}{e} \approx 1.156$.

blocks.name: cplx-contour
blocks.cap: The same picture with $\cos z$: now the arc grows as you drag the handle out, because $\cos(iy) = \cosh y$ blows up. That is why $\cos z$ is the wrong function to integrate.

blocks.title: A sine integral
steps: Use $f(z) = \frac{ze^{iz}}{z^2 + 9}$; the upper pole is $3i$. Here the top has degree only one less, so Jordan's lemma is needed for the arc.
The sine integral is the imaginary part: $\pi e^{-3}$.

items: Replace $\cos(ax)$ or $\sin(ax)$ by $e^{iaz}$ (with $a > 0$).
Find the poles of $R(z)$ in the upper half-plane and the residues of $R(z)e^{iaz}$ there.
Multiply the sum by $2\pi i$; take the real part for cosine, the imaginary part for sine.

blocks.title: A residue to check
blocks.q: Find the residue of $\dfrac{e^{3iz}}{z^2 + 4}$ at $z = 2i$, and use it to evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\cos 3x}{x^2 + 4}\,dx$.
steps: $2\pi i\cdot\frac{e^{-6}}{4i} = \frac{\pi e^{-6}}{2}$, which matches $\frac{\pi e^{-kb}}{b}$ with $k = 3$, $b = 2$.

blocks.html: Replacing $\cos x$ by $\cos z$. On the real line they agree, but in the upper half-plane $\cos z = \frac{e^{iz} + e^{-iz}}{2}$ contains $e^{-iz}$, whose size is $e^{y}$: it explodes on the arc, and the arc integral does not vanish. Integrate $R(z)e^{iaz}$ (with $a > 0$, so the exponential decays upward) and take the real or imaginary part at the end. If $a < 0$, close in the lower half-plane instead.

blocks.html: Apply the residue theorem to the logarithmic derivative $\frac{f'}{f}$. Its residues are exactly the orders of the zeros and poles of $f$, so the integral counts them, and it also measures how many times the image curve $f(C)$ winds around $0$.

Argument principle. If $f$ is analytic on and inside $C$ except for finitely many poles inside, and has no zeros or poles on $C$, then $$\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_C\frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}\,dz = Z - P,$$ where $Z$ and $P$ count the zeros and the poles inside $C$, each counted with its multiplicity. This number is also the number of times $f(C)$ winds around $0$ (counterclockwise positive).

Near a zero of order $m$, $f = (z - a)^mg$ with $g(a) \ne 0$, so $\frac{f'}{f} = \frac{m}{z - a} + \frac{g'}{g}$: residue $m$. Near a pole of order $m$, $f = (z - a)^{-m}g$ and the residue is $-m$. Adding up gives $Z - P$. On the other hand, $\frac{f'}{f} = \frac{d}{dz}\log f$, so the integral measures the total change of $\log f(z)$ around $C$: the change in $\ln|f|$ is $0$, and the change in $\arg f$ is $2\pi$ times the winding number of $f(C)$ around $0$.

blocks.name: cplx-winding
blocks.cap: Left: the circle $C$ and the zeros of $z^3 - 2z + 1$ (dots; those inside are green). Right: the image curve $f(C)$. Press Play: the counter of turns around $0$ ends at the number of zeros inside. Resize $C$ to change the count.

blocks.title: Counting with multiplicity
steps: $Z - P = 2 - 3 = -1$: the image curve winds once clockwise around $0$.

blocks.title: A power
blocks.q: How many times does $f(C)$ wind around $0$ for $f(z) = z^5$ and $C$: $|z| = 1$?
steps: $z = e^{it}$ gives $f = e^{5it}$: the image goes around the unit circle $5$ times.
Also $Z - P = 5 - 0$ (a zero of order $5$ at $0$).

blocks.html: In practice the winding number is often read off a picture of $f(C)$, or estimated numerically, and then the argument principle tells you how many zeros lie inside: a standard way to locate roots of polynomials and to test the stability of control systems.

Counting a zero once regardless of its multiplicity, or forgetting the poles. A double zero contributes $2$, a triple pole contributes $-3$. In the first example, counting "one zero, one pole" would give $0$ instead of $-1$. Write each zero and pole with its order next to it before adding.

blocks.html: The argument principle counts zeros by winding numbers. Rouché's theorem turns that into a quick comparison: if one part of a function dominates the rest on a circle, the whole function has as many zeros inside as that part alone.

Rouché's theorem. If $f$ and $g$ are analytic on and inside a simple closed contour $C$, and $$|g(z)| < |f(z)| \quad\text{at every point of } C,$$ then $f$ and $f + g$ have the same number of zeros inside $C$ (counted with multiplicity).

Picture a person walking along the curve $f(C)$ around a post at $0$, with a dog on a leash: the dog's position is $f + g$, and the leash has length $|g|$. Since the leash is always shorter than the person's distance $|f|$ to the post, the dog can never reach the post, so both go around it the same number of times. By the argument principle, those winding numbers are the zero counts of $f$ and of $f + g$.

blocks.cap: $f = z^5$ (walker, blue curve) and $f + g = z^5 + 3z + 1$ (dog, green curve) on $|z| = 2$: $|g| \le 7 < 32 = |f|$, so both wind $5$ times. Shrink the circle to radius $1$: now the inequality fails, and the theorem says nothing with $f = z^5$ (try $f = 3z$ in your head instead).

blocks.title: Inside the unit circle
blocks.q: How many zeros does $p(z) = z^5 + 6z^2 - 1$ have in $|z| < 1$?
steps: $2 < 6$ on the whole circle, so $p$ has as many zeros inside as $6z^2$: two.

blocks.title: A larger circle
blocks.q: How many zeros does $p(z) = z^5 + 6z^2 - 1$ have in $|z| < 2$?
steps: Combined with the previous example: $5 - 2 = 3$ zeros lie in the annulus $1 \le |z| < 2$ (none on $|z| = 1$, where $|p| \ge 6 - 2 > 0$).

blocks.title: No zeros
blocks.q: Show that $z^4 + z + 5$ has no zeros in $|z| < 1$.
steps: The constant $5$ has no zeros, so neither does $z^4 + z + 5$ inside the circle.

blocks.html: Checking the inequality at one point, or picking the wrong main term. $|g| < |f|$ must hold at every point of $C$, so bound $|g|$ by its worst case (the triangle inequality adds the largest sizes of its terms). And choose $f$ as the term that wins on that circle: on $|z| = 1$ the term $6z^2$ wins for $z^5 + 6z^2 - 1$, but on $|z| = 2$ the top power $z^5$ does. If no single term beats the sum of the others, try a different circle.

blocks.html: Near a point where it is analytic, a function acts like multiplication by the number $f'(z_0)$: a turn and a uniform stretch. Mappings with that property keep the angles between curves, and that makes them the tool of choice for moving a hard problem (heat flow, fluid flow, electric fields) from an awkward region to a simple one.

An analytic $f$ is conformal at $z_0$ when $f'(z_0) \ne 0$: any two smooth curves through $z_0$ that meet at an angle $\alpha$ have images that meet at the same angle $\alpha$, with the same orientation. Small shapes near $z_0$ are turned by $\arg f'(z_0)$ and scaled by $|f'(z_0)|$ (areas by $|f'(z_0)|^2$).
Where $f'(z_0) = 0$, angles are not kept: if the first nonzero derivative there is $f^{(n)}$, angles at $z_0$ are multiplied by $n$.

A curve $z(t)$ through $z_0 = z(0)$ has tangent direction $z'(0)$. Its image $f(z(t))$ has tangent $f'(z_0)\,z'(0)$ by the chain rule. Multiplying by the same nonzero complex number $f'(z_0)$ turns every tangent by the same angle $\arg f'(z_0)$, so the angle between two tangents is unchanged. When $f'(z_0) = 0$ and $f(z) \approx f(z_0) + c(z - z_0)^n$ with $c \ne 0$, the map behaves like $(z - z_0)^n$, which multiplies angles at $z_0$ by $n$.

blocks.cap: Two segments through $z_0$ at $45^\circ$ and their images under $z^2$: still $45^\circ$ apart (readout). Now drag $z_0$ to $0$, where $f'(0) = 0$: the angle between the images doubles to $90^\circ$.

blocks.title: Turn and stretch
blocks.q: For $f(z) = z^2$ at $z_0 = 1 + i$, find the angle by which small shapes are turned and the factor by which they are stretched.

blocks.title: Where a map fails to be conformal
steps: $f' = 0$ at $z = \pm 1$. There $f''(\pm 1) = \pm 6 \ne 0$, so angles at those points are doubled. Everywhere else $f$ is conformal.

blocks.title: Angles at a critical point
blocks.q: Two rays leave $0$ at an angle of $\frac{\pi}{6}$. At what angle do their images under $w = z^3$ leave $0$?
steps: A ray $\arg z = \theta$ goes to $\arg w = 3\theta$.

blocks.html: Expecting angles to be kept where $f' = 0$. Conformality needs $f'(z_0) \ne 0$. The map $z^2$ is analytic everywhere, but at $0$ it doubles every angle: the positive real and positive imaginary axes (a right angle) go to the positive and negative real axes (a straight angle). Before claiming a map keeps angles at a point, compute $f'$ there.

blocks.html: The simplest conformal maps beyond $az + b$ are quotients of linear functions. They are conformal everywhere they are defined, they can be undone, and they have one striking geometric property: they never bend a circle into anything but a circle or a line.

A Möbius transformation is $T(z) = \dfrac{az + b}{cz + d}$ with $ad - bc \ne 0$. When $c \ne 0$, $T$ sends $-\frac{d}{c}$ to $\infty$ and $\infty$ to $\frac{a}{c}$; its inverse is $T^{-1}(w) = \dfrac{dw - b}{-cw + a}$. Every Möbius map sends circles and lines to circles and lines: the image of a circle or line is a line exactly when it passes through $-\frac{d}{c}$.

$T'(z) = \frac{ad - bc}{(cz + d)^2} \ne 0$, so $T$ is conformal wherever it is defined. Divide out: $T(z) = \frac{a}{c} + \frac{bc - ad}{c}\cdot\frac{1}{cz + d}$, so $T$ is a chain of a linear map, the inversion $\frac{1}{z}$, and another linear map. Linear maps send circles to circles and lines to lines. For $\frac{1}{z}$, a circle or line has an equation $A|z|^2 + B\operatorname{Re} z + C\operatorname{Im} z + D = 0$; replacing $z$ by $\frac{1}{w}$ and multiplying by $|w|^2$ gives $A + B\operatorname{Re} w - C\operatorname{Im} w + D|w|^2 = 0$, the same kind of equation. It is a line exactly when $D = 0$, that is, when the original passes through $0$, the point inversion sends to $\infty$.

blocks.name: cplx-mapping
blocks.cap: $T(z) = \frac{z}{z - 1}$ sends the unit circle (which passes through $1 = -\frac{d}{c}$) to the vertical line $\operatorname{Re} w = \frac{1}{2}$. Drag $z_0$ around the circle and watch $w_0$ run along the line.

blocks.title: Special points
blocks.q: For $T(z) = \dfrac{2z + i}{z - 3}$, find $T(0)$, the point sent to $\infty$, and $T(\infty)$.

blocks.html: Composing two Möbius maps gives another one, and the coefficients compose like $2 \times 2$ matrices: $\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}$. The inverse map corresponds to the inverse matrix (up to a scalar), which is where the formula $\frac{dw - b}{-cw + a}$ comes from.

Expecting every circle to map to a circle. Möbius maps send circles to circles or lines. If a circle passes through $-\frac{d}{c}$, one of its points goes to $\infty$, and a "circle through $\infty$" is a line. Check: plug $-\frac{d}{c}$ into the circle's equation. For $T(z) = \frac{z}{z - 1}$, the unit circle passes through $1$, so its image is a line.

blocks.html: A Möbius map has four coefficients, but scaling all of them by the same number changes nothing, so it has three degrees of freedom. Choosing where three points go uses them all up: there is exactly one Möbius map for each choice.

Given distinct $z_1, z_2, z_3$, the map $$S(z) = \frac{(z - z_1)(z_2 - z_3)}{(z - z_3)(z_2 - z_1)}$$ is the unique Möbius map with $S(z_1) = 0$, $S(z_2) = 1$, $S(z_3) = \infty$. (If one $z_j$ is $\infty$, drop the two factors containing it.) To send $z_1, z_2, z_3$ to $w_1, w_2, w_3$, solve $$\frac{(w - w_1)(w_2 - w_3)}{(w - w_3)(w_2 - w_1)} = \frac{(z - z_1)(z_2 - z_3)}{(z - z_3)(z_2 - z_1)}$$ for $w$. These quotients are cross-ratios, which Möbius maps preserve.

Check $S$ directly: the factor $z - z_1$ makes $S(z_1) = 0$, the factor $z - z_3$ in the bottom makes $S(z_3) = \infty$, and at $z = z_2$ everything cancels to $1$. Uniqueness: if $T$ also sends $z_1, z_2, z_3$ to $0, 1, \infty$, then $T \circ S^{-1}$ fixes $0$, $1$ and $\infty$; fixing $\infty$ and $0$ forces the form $kz$, and fixing $1$ forces $k = 1$. For general targets, if $S_z$ and $S_w$ send the triples to $0, 1, \infty$, the map is $S_w^{-1} \circ S_z$, which is what the cross-ratio equation says.

blocks.cap: Drag $z_1, z_2, z_3$: the map sending them to $0, 1, \infty$ is rebuilt each time, its formula is shown, and the circle through the three points (dashed) always lands on the real axis.

blocks.title: To $0$, $1$, $infty$
blocks.q: Find the Möbius map with $T(1) = 0$, $T(i) = 1$, $T(-1) = \infty$, and compute $T(0)$.

blocks.title: With $infty$ among the points
steps: Fixing $\infty$ means no denominator: $T(z) = Az + B$.

blocks.title: General targets
blocks.q: Find the Möbius map with $0 \mapsto 1$, $1 \mapsto i$, $\infty \mapsto -1$, and compute $T(-1)$.
steps: Cross-ratio with $z_3 = \infty$: the right side is $\frac{z - 0}{1 - 0} = z$. The left side is $\frac{(w - 1)(i + 1)}{(w + 1)(i - 1)} = -i\,\frac{w - 1}{w + 1}$.
Solve $-i\frac{w - 1}{w + 1} = z$: $\frac{w - 1}{w + 1} = iz$, so $w = \frac{1 + iz}{1 - iz}$.

blocks.html: Three points determine a circle (or a line, if they are collinear). The map $S$ sends that circle onto the extended real line, since it sends the three points to $0$, $1$ and $\infty$, which lie on it. This is the quickest way to find which region a Möbius map sends onto a half-plane.

Pairing the points in the wrong order. The formula assigns roles: $z_1 \mapsto 0$, $z_2 \mapsto 1$, $z_3 \mapsto \infty$. Swapping two points gives a different map. In the first example, sending $1, -1, i$ to $0, 1, \infty$ instead gives $T(0) = \frac{-1 \cdot (-1 - i)}{-i \cdot (-2)} = \frac{1 + i}{2i}$, not $i$. Check your map on all three given points before using it.

blocks.html: To solve a problem on an awkward region, map the region onto a simple one, usually the unit disk or the upper half-plane. A small toolkit covers many cases: powers open or close sectors, the exponential unrolls strips, and Möbius maps trade half-planes for disks.

• $w = \dfrac{z - i}{z + i}$ maps the upper half-plane onto the unit disk $|w| < 1$ (with $i \mapsto 0$); its inverse is $z = i\,\dfrac{1 + w}{1 - w}$.
• $w = z^n$ maps the sector $0 < \arg z < \frac{\pi}{n}$ onto the upper half-plane.
• $w = e^{\pi z/a}$ maps the horizontal strip $0 < \operatorname{Im} z < a$ onto the upper half-plane.
Chain them: map onto an intermediate region first, then onto the target.

For the first map, $|w| = \frac{|z - i|}{|z + i|}$ compares the distance from $z$ to $i$ with the distance to $-i$. A point in the upper half-plane is closer to $i$, so $|w| < 1$; on the real axis the distances are equal, so the boundary goes to the unit circle. For $z^n$, angles multiply by $n$, so the sector's opening $\frac{\pi}{n}$ becomes $\pi$. For the strip, $e^{x + iy}$ sends the line at height $y$ to the ray at angle $y$; heights $0$ to $\pi$ give the upper half-plane, and rescaling by $\frac{\pi}{a}$ fits a strip of height $a$ to that.

blocks.cap: $\frac{z - i}{z + i}$ sends the upper half-plane (left) onto the unit disk (right). The point $i$ goes to the center; drag $z_0$ toward the real axis and $w_0$ moves out to the circle.

blocks.title: A point of the half-plane
steps: Check: $|w|^2 = \frac{4 + 1}{25} = \frac{1}{5} < 1$, inside the disk as it should be.

blocks.title: A strip
blocks.q: Find $k > 0$ so that $e^{kz}$ maps the strip $0 < \operatorname{Im} z < 2$ onto the upper half-plane.
steps: $e^{\zeta}$ handles a strip of height $\pi$, so stretch heights by $k = \frac{\pi}{2}$.

blocks.title: A chain of maps
blocks.q: Map the first quadrant onto the unit disk, and find the image of $z = 1 + i$.
steps: $\zeta = z^2$ opens the quadrant ($0 < \arg z < \frac{\pi}{2}$) into the upper half-plane.
$w = \frac{\zeta - i}{\zeta + i}$ then maps it onto the disk. Together: $w = \frac{z^2 - i}{z^2 + i}$.

blocks.html: In applications the order is: map the awkward region onto the upper half-plane or the disk, solve the problem there (where the answer is often known in closed form), and map the solution back. Because the maps are conformal, harmonic functions stay harmonic along the way.

Checking the boundary but not the inside. $\frac{z - i}{z + i}$ and $\frac{z + i}{z - i}$ both send the real axis onto the unit circle, but the first sends the upper half-plane inside the disk and the second sends it outside. After matching boundaries, test one interior point: here $i \mapsto 0$, inside the disk, so the first map is the right one.
